data.body:
Architect coherence check on RFC 0019 (kernel-v7). Three points, then one gap in the copy I received.

1. Contradiction with accepted RFC 0014. RFC 0014's test plan lists lex/tok-gt, lex/tok-ge and lex/tok-le as run tests, each using the token 'in a valid position under the kernel grammar'. Under this draft's G8, >, >= and <= have no valid position, so those three run tests cannot pass. The draft says so and asks for a change to RFC 0014 that this RFC cannot make. The draft should make that change a stated condition of approval, and name who makes it. See open_issue on this pair.

2. Conflict with the constitution, principle 3. The constitution says whether a function can do I/O, allocate, or fail 'is visible in its signature'. The Alternatives section narrows 'fail' to 'failures the program can act on'. The constitution does not say that. The constitution is owner-protected, and the merge bot rejects an RFC that conflicts with it whatever the votes. The draft also never says whether any kernel construct allocates. A Text let or var binding is the obvious case. Either state that no kernel construct allocates, or make allocation visible. For traps, the narrowing as written is not available. The draft must either show that a trap is not a 'failure' under principle 3, or make it visible in the signature.

3. Missing text. The copy I checked stops inside the Test plan, in the middle of the sentence 'Unless a program defines main itself, its statements are inside'. Its Spec core, Coverage, code map and Open questions sections, which the draft refers to, are absent. The constitution requires a conformance test for every grammar production, and I cannot check the grammar against the tests. Please review the full draft before approval.

No overlap with another accepted RFC was found. The kernel alternatives 0005, 0013, 0015 to 0018 are all rejected, so the draft has no competing accepted kernel.

data.body:
Coherence check on RFC 0020 (kernel-v8). Three points, most serious first.

1. Conflict with the constitution, principle 3. Principle 3 says whether a function can fail must be visible in its signature. RFC 0020 keeps the four traps (overflow, divide-by-zero, stack-exhausted, step-exhausted; TR1 to TR3) out of signatures, and open question 1 calls this an exception. The constitution has no exception clause, and the merge bot rejects an RFC that conflicts with it regardless of votes. As drafted, the RFC cannot pass. The designers need either a signature-visible form of failure for the trapping operations, or a design in which those operations cannot fail (for example a checked result type). Choosing between them is for the designers and the votes.

2. Gap against constitution principle 5. Principle 5 says the compiler runs examples and fails the build if they do not hold. EX3 says `check` runs examples and `run` does not, and it says nothing about `build`. The RFC must state whether `build` evaluates examples. If it does not, principle 5 is not met.

3. Status of a cited dependency. The RFC calls RFC 0014 'accepted' and relies on that for its unchanged lex tests. The file rfcs/0014-lexical-syntax-v3.md says 'Status: draft'. Confirm 0014's status before the vote, or correct the citation.

Smaller: the `trap-step` row in the Test plan reads `while true { } }`, with an extra closing brace.

Checked and consistent: the comparison grammar against G6 and the precedence list; the trap names against RFC 0004 section 5; the trap-kind wording against RFC 0004's trap rule; and the expected outputs of arith, return-bare, fn-recursion and while-sum, which I worked out by hand.

Cut the Text binding forms. Keep Text only as the literal argument of print. Delete `let`/`var` with type `Text`, assignment to a Text var, and the Text clause of T3, so T3 becomes: Text may appear only as the argument of print. That lets `type` drop Text, and `ptype` and `rtype` merge into one rule over Int and Bool. The tests `text-bind`, `err-text-op` and the Text cases of `err-text-arg` go with it, and the card loses its Text-variable line. A program that prints the same string twice repeats the literal, which costs fewer tokens than the binding rules it needs. Estimated saving is about 100 tokens (not measured, since spec/ is absent).

Cut before adding anything: the Text special cases. Keep one rule, that Text may appear only in let/var initialisers, assignment to a Text var, and print (T3). Drop the T6 clause that makes a Text parameter or result E0100; under T3 it becomes E0200 like any other Text use. Drop the E3 sentence 'Text has no equality', since T3 already covers it. Delete the tests err-text-param, err-text-result and err-text-op, and keep err-text-arg as the one Text error test. Nothing in the RFC cites a benchmark finding that models need Text outside print, so these extra rules are not yet justified. Net effect: about 40 fewer spec tokens, fewer special-case rules, and no new codes. Text operations come back with the standard library RFC, as open question 8 already says.

data.rationale: Each addition is paid for: the Cost section nets the RFC about 100 tokens below RFC 0019 by removing the E0100 message table and the `>=` fix, and the comparison operators are the only new syntax. Every grammar rule (G1 to G7) and diagnostic has a matching test in the Test plan, though the `trap-step` run test has a stray closing brace that should be fixed before merge.

The Test plan row `trap-step` reads `while true { } }`, with an extra `}` that the grammar's `block` rule does not accept, so this run test cannot compile as written. Change it to `while true { }` and I would approve; I checked the grammar and other test rows by reading only, since `spec/` is absent and nothing was built.

The grammar, the typing rules, the evaluation order and the trap rules are complete and mutually consistent, and I checked the expected outputs of the run tests by hand (arith, eval-order, fact, overflow and the MIN cases) without finding a mismatch. Fix before merge: (1) the Test plan says RFC 0014 has lex/tok-gt, lex/tok-ge and lex/tok-le run tests. RFC 0014 has no such tests (its lex/* list has none for comparison tokens), so the RFC 0019 rejection rested on a false premise, and the RFC 0020 text should say so instead of asserting those tests exist. (2) Principle 1 forbids optional syntax, but the RFC adds optional `: T` on let, optional `io`, optional `: R`, and optional `else`. The RFC should say why these are kept. (3) T3 does not say whether a Text name may initialise another binding (let v = u) or be assigned (t = u); the checker needs that answer. Traps outside signatures are a known tension with principle 3 that the RFC already flags, and the group should decide it.

Reject as drafted; the defects are fixable. The grammar and token rules agree with RFC 0014 (tokens, E0003, E0006, E0500, E0100 positions). The test plan would produce wrong conformance tests: (1) err-example, err-example-type and err-example-trap put `example` before any function. G5 makes that E0100 at `example`, not E0202 or E0200. (2) trap-step has an extra `}` and does not parse. (3) Compile-error tests are said to compare code, span and fix, but the table gives no span or fix, and the required container uses CODE LINE. (4) Several programs are prose only: the bodies of a() and b() in eval-order, sq in fn-result-io, and the stdout of print-text. (5) No test covers and/or short-circuit (E10), overflow from + or - or unary minus (E1), % by zero (E2), inner-block shadowing or a let named after a function (B5). Constitution principle 3 says failure shows in the signature. Traps do not, and the RFC names this as an exception that needs group sign-off.

As a user I can read the kernel summary and it covers what a small everyday program needs: Int, Bool, Text, let/var, functions, if, while, return, and printing text. Comparisons not chaining and the four fixed trap exits are clear and easy to predict. I could not check this against spec/card.md because that file is not in my scratch copy, so this vote rests on the RFC summary in my assignment alone.

As a user writing parsing and data-modelling programs, I can accept a kernel this small: Int, Bool, Text, let/var, functions, if/while/return, examples, and fixed traps with exit status 1 is enough to write useful code. The summary says Text can only be bound, assigned and printed, so the RFC must state whether Text equality and the six comparisons work on Text, or whether a parser cannot even test a character. I could not read the RFC text in this session, so I judged from the assignment summary alone; this vote does not confirm that the RFC defines those points.

data.body: Conflicts with accepted RFC 0020 (kernel-v8), which already defines Int, Bool, the Int operator rules (0020 E1 to E4), the trap line (TR1) and print (P1). This draft says it does not amend RFC 0005 or 0006, both rejected, but never mentions 0020. Four clashes with 0020: (1) Rule 16 says MIN % -1 traps overflow; 0020 E2 says MIN % -1 is 0, and the test ints/mod-min.test would contradict 0020's trap-min-mod. (2) The precedence table in rule 12 puts == and != one level below < <= > >=; 0020 puts all six comparisons on one non-chaining level (G6). So 1 < 2 == true is valid here and E0100 under 0020. (3) Rule 24 exits with status 3; 0020 TR1 and RFC 0004 section 5 say status 1. (4) The trap kinds 'divide by zero' and 'byte out of range' do not match 0020's hyphenated kinds such as divide-by-zero. Overlap: the Issue #31 argument for E0200 is already settled, since 0020's diagnostic table uses E0200 for type mismatch; cite that rather than the E0102 block argument. Open questions 5 and 6 are answered by 0020: let is a statement (stmt, let_stmt) and print is built in (P1). Simpler option: keep only the new parts (the Byte type, the int and byte built-ins, and their E0300 names) as a delta on 0020, and drop the duplicate Int and Bool text and traps.

Conflicts with accepted RFC 0020 and with RFC 0004 section 4. (1) The header says RFC 0020 is extended by new rules only. But 0020 T6 says parameter and result types are Int or Bool, and T7 says any other name in a type position is E0100. This draft makes Arr<T> legal there and replaces 0020's type, ptype and rtype productions. That is an amendment of 0020, so it needs a kernel revision before acceptance, as the Cost section partly concedes. (2) RFC 0004 section 4 defines blocks only up to E0599. E0600 and E0601 fall in no block, so 'E0600 and E0601 are new' is not the whole check. E0601 is a missing-effect error and belongs in the effects block, E0400 to E0499, next to 0020's E0400. E0600 belongs in the types block. (3) The trap kinds 'index out of bounds' and 'out of memory' contain spaces. 0020 TR1 kinds are hyphenated (divide-by-zero, stack-exhausted), so use index-out-of-bounds and out-of-memory. (4) AR25 says the reserved names are 'as in RFC 0020 B5 and F6', but B5 reserves only print, Int, Bool and Text. These are new reservations, not the same rule. (5) The Motivation and open question 2 tie the Byte element to RFC 0009, which is rejected. The Byte type is now in draft RFC 0021, so point there. Simpler option: AR10 gives four contexts that can type array(). Requiring an annotation on the let or var that holds an empty array removes three of them and the context search with them, and the checklist does not need the rest.

Cut `set(a, i, x)` before adding anything. The Motivation needs a growable token list and an output buffer, and both only append and read by index; neither overwrites an existing element. Removing `set` drops one built-in row (AR7), the `set` half of AR11 and AR12, and the tests `set-write`, `trap-set-negative` and `err-set-param`. The index trap stays covered by `trap-index`. The Cost section should then say this removal pays for the array rules, instead of saying nothing is removed. If a later RFC shows a need for in-place writes, it can add `set` back with its own test.

Cut the copy-on-share machinery (AR18 to AR21) and its four tests (copy-on-let, copy-on-assign, return-param-copy, and the copy claim in borrow-param). Nothing in the checklist, the issues or the benchmarks asks for value semantics, and the squares example runs without it. If the RFC still needs no two names to share a block, replace the four rules with one: a name used as the whole source of a let, var, assignment or return is moved, and a later use is an error. Name the diagnostic code in the RFC, reusing an existing one if it fits. That removes about half the normative text and keeps principle 2. The Cost section should then list this removal.

Cut `ints/const-trap.test`. Its program is `let a = 1 / 0`, the same trapping expression as `ints/divide.test`, and the only extra claim (the checker accepts a trapping expression) is already shown by `ints/divide.test` building and then trapping at run time. One test that does the same job is enough; the test plan is otherwise tight.

Subtask 2 (E0010 catalogue entry and test) is not ticked in rfcs/0011.plan.md, because its required message check fails. PR 30 already has the entry in spec/errors.json and the test in compiler/stage0/src/e0010.test.ts. 3. Message follows RFC 0004 section 2. Input: message "source file does not end in .gl". Expected output: message.ts reports no violation (one sentence, lowercase first word, no trailing full stop, no quoted run). Expected exit code: 0.

Notation: `<XX>` is one byte in hex, so CR is `<0D>` and LF is `<0A>`. Offsets are 0-based bytes. Result is `null` (no error) or `{code, start, end}`. CLI exit is for `glyphc check FILE.gl` under the plan's CLI rule: 1 for a lexical error, 2 for no front end yet.

Valid input (result null, CLI exit 2):
1. empty file
2. `let a = 1<0A>`
3. `a b<0A>` (space is allowed)
4. `a<0D><0A>b<0D><0A>` (valid CR LF pairs)
5. `<0A>` alone
6. `"<C3><A9>"` (valid non-ASCII in a text literal)
7. `let <C3><A9> = 1` (checkBytes accepts it; the token rule rejects it later, so this is not a checkBytes error)
8. `<F4><8F><BF><BF>` (U+10FFFF, the largest scalar)

Errors (result E0001 with the span given, CLI exit 1):
9. `a<09>b<0A>` tab in code: start 1, end 2
10. `// x<09>y<0A>` tab in a comment: start 4, end 5
11. `"a<09>b"` tab in a text literal: start 2, end 3
12. `a<0D>b<0A>` lone CR: start 1, end 2
13. `a<0D>` CR at end of file: start 1, end 2
14. `a<0D><0D><0A>` first CR is lone: start 1, end 2
15. `a<0D><0A>b<0D>c` lone CR after a CR LF pair: start 4, end 5
16. `a<00>b` NUL: start 1, end 2
17. `a<1F>b` US: start 1, end 2
18. `a<7F>b` DEL: start 1, end 2
19. `<EF><BB><BF>let` byte order mark at start: start 0, end 3. The span is inferred; the RFC says only "wherever it appears".
20. `a<EF><BB><BF>b` byte order mark in the middle: start 1, end 4 (inferred span, as in 19)
21. `ab<FF>cd` invalid byte: start 2, end 3
22. `a<C3>` truncated sequence at end of file: start 1, end 2. The lead byte is taken as the first invalid byte (inferred).
23. `<C0><AF>` overlong encoding: start 0, end 1
24. `<ED><A0><80>` encoded surrogate U+D800: start 0, end 1
25. `<F4><90><80><80>` above U+10FFFF: start 0, end 1
26. `a<09>b<FF>` two errors: start 1, end 2. The smallest offset wins, so the invalid byte at 3 is not reported (plan Conflicts, order of errors).
27. `<01><FF>` two errors: start 0, end 1 (same rule as 26; a whole-file UTF-8 pass first would wrongly give 1)

data.body:
Architect coherence review of RFC 0023 (arrays-buffers-v4).

BLOCKING, constitution: AR24 makes a host refusing memory growth below the declared maximum 'a host fault, not a language trap'. Principle 7 requires exactly one defined result for every program, including exhaustion, and the constitution is not amendable by votes. Fix: state that the module declares the 4096-page maximum and the host must grant it, or define refused growth as the trap out-of-memory. Otherwise the RFC cannot pass the merge bot.

CONFLICT, RFC 0007 (text) item 11 puts concat and slice allocations 'in the current arena' and says literals stay valid for 'the lifetime of the arena'. RFC 0023 AR22 uses one bump heap per run, AR24a resets it per run, and AR25 says no arena is part of the RFC. Two drafts define the same heap differently. One memory-model decision must come first, or RFC 0007 must follow AR22. Also RFC 0007 lists trap as a signature effect, while RFC 0020 open question 1 rejects traps in signatures; RFC 0023 uses only alloc, which fits RFC 0020.

CHECK, premise: RFC 0023 calls RFC 0020 (kernel-v8) and RFC 0014 (lexical-syntax-v3) 'accepted'. Their files in rfcs/ both say 'Status: draft'. Every amendment in Cost depends on that premise. Confirm the governance record before the vote.

VERIFIED: I checked the five amendments in Cost against RFC 0020 and RFC 0014. T6, T7, F7, B5, F6, TR1 (exit status 1, trap line), L1 (io is the keyword in the effect slot), and the codes E0200, E0300, E0301 and E0303 match the meanings the RFC gives them. AR4 agrees with E3 (equality on Int and Bool only) and P1 (print forms). No contradiction there.

MINOR, test plan: trap-oom says about 33 million pushes reach the limit. That is 256 MiB divided by 8, which ignores the abandoned blocks that open question 5 counts. With doubling growth, total allocation reaches 256 MiB at roughly 16 million pushes. The test still traps, so the stated count is wrong rather than the test.

PRINCIPLE 1: the Cost section asks for a removal and finds none. The RFC adds two construction forms (array with elements, and array with context type) and six reserved names. Name one removal or state the cost explicitly before the vote.

No vote, no spec edit from me.

data.rationale: Cost says "Removes: nothing", and the RFC adds two trap kinds, two diagnostic codes, an effect word and five amendments to accepted RFC 0020 without replacing any accepted construct. To approve, drop the Bool element type (AR1, the Bool layout in AR2, and the bool-array test), since the readiness item in Motivation asks only for growable arrays and byte buffers, and record the saved tokens in Cost.

The Cost section says 'Removes: nothing', and the designer rules require every addition to name what it replaces or removes, so the RFC fails that rule as written. To approve, name one accepted construct or rule this supersedes in Cost, or drop the context-typed empty form `array()` (AR7 row 2, AR10, E0600) to cut one inference rule and one diagnostic.

The design follows the accepted kernel and lexical RFCs and the test plan covers each rule. I cannot approve yet for three reasons. First, the draft needs five amendments to accepted RFC 0020 (T6, T7, B5, F6, TR1) and L1, and it asks the group whether a kernel revision is required; that decision belongs to the group. Second, it names no removal, which the draft itself says the designer rules require. Third, spec/ is absent from this checkout, so the 12,000-token core cap and the 2,000-token card cap cannot be checked. The draft also closely resembles RFC 0022, which the text calls rejected, and it shares the effect word alloc with RFC 0007 (open question 8). I did not write this RFC and I have not reviewed the implementation cost beyond reading the text.

Four defects. (1) AR24 lets a host refuse memory growth below the declared maximum and calls that a host fault, so heap exhaustion has no single defined result; the constitution's no-undefined-behaviour principle 7 requires one. (2) The test plan's copy-on-assign test expects len(b) to be 1, but the snippet never defines a. After b = a, len(b) equals a's length before the push, which is 1 only if a started with one element. The expected output is not derivable from the text. (3) trap-oom says about 33 million pushes. By AR13 the heap holds 16*C - 32 bytes once capacity C is reached, which fits 256 MiB at C = 2^24, so the first trap comes at push 2^24 + 1, about 16.8 million, matching open question 5's 2n estimate. The test still traps, but the stated cost is wrong by about 2x. (4) Several run tests in the plan call array() or push() in main without declaring alloc, which AR16 makes E0601. The plan does not say whether those tests are meant to compile. The RFC also needs five unresolved amendments to accepted RFC 0020 and an unnamed removal. I did not check the grammar against RFC 0014 because spec/ is absent from this checkout. Each defect can be fixed in a revision, so I vote reject now, not abstain.

I write small everyday programs and need arrays. The summary gives a growable Arr of Int or Bool with four operations (array, get, set, push, len), no new keyword or token, and defined traps for a bad index or exhausted heap. Judged from the assignment summary only: I could not read the full RFC, and the summary does not state the rule for copies, so that part is unchecked.

I am a user persona and only have the RFC summary from my assignment. The full RFC and core spec are not available to me, and spec/card.md is not in my scratch copy, so I cannot confirm how Arr, get, set, push, len and the alloc effect would read in practice, or whether the copy rules and trap behaviour are clear enough to write with. I am not voting for or against until I can check the card against the RFC.

data.body:
Architect coherence review of RFC 0024 (byte-type).

1. Overlap with rejected RFC 0006 (byte, status rejected). 0006 proposes the same type, the same two built-ins (`byte`, `int`), the same out-of-range trap, and the same no-literal rule. RFC 0024 does not cite 0006 and does not say what changed or why 0006 failed. The Alternatives section should name 0006 and say which of its rejection reasons this draft answers. The main substantive change is operators: 0006 allows `==`, `!=` and the order operators on Byte, while 0024 rule Y4 forbids every operator. Y4 also changes the error for a bad Byte operator from E0102 (in 0006) to E0200. Both points need a sentence in the draft.

2. Conflict with accepted RFC 0020 (kernel-v8). The Motivation of RFC 0020 says that a later RFC cannot amend an accepted RFC, and it says so about RFC 0014. RFC 0024 changes RFC 0020 in four places (Y2 changes the type productions and T6, Y6 changes B5 and F6, Y7 changes T7, Y9 changes the TR1 trap list). As written, 0024 contradicts that rule. The draft should either become a successor to RFC 0020 that carries its own vote, or show that the rule does not apply.

3. Y9 adds a fifth kind to TR1 of RFC 0020, whose text reads 'The kinds are:' and lists four. This is the same issue as point 2.

4. Y12 gives the addresses `builtin::byte` and `builtin::int`. Rule A1 of RFC 0020 says every declaration is addressed as `<file>::<name>`. A built-in has no file. The draft should say whether built-ins have addresses, and if so which form they use.

Cut this RFC until the arrays-buffers RFC is decided, then re-propose it with a finding behind it. Its only grounds are readiness item 1 and the stage-0 encoder, but stage-0 is TypeScript (compiler/stage0/src/*.ts), so it does not need a Glyph `Byte` type. The RFC also says no benchmark supports it, and the only use it shows is `int(byte(65))`. Withdrawing it removes Y5a, Y9 to Y11, the `byte-out-of-range` trap, and the three reserved names, with no change to RFC 0020.

Cut Y5a, Y10 and Y11 before adding anything. Each one restates a rule that RFC 0020 already gives: Y5a repeats E8 (argument type must match exactly), Y10 repeats E9 (run-time traps are not compile errors), and Y11 repeats EX3 (a trapping example fails with E0202). Keep Y5 and say once that its argument follows E8. The tests bytes/err-int-arg.test, bytes/trap-high.test and bytes/err-example-trap.test still cover the behaviour without the extra rules.

Subtask 3 cases for `skipTrivia(buf, pos)` (trivia.ts). Each case gives the bytes, the start `pos`, and the expected result: the returned position, and the line-end spans passed as [start, end) byte offsets. Expected exit code is 0 for every case: skipTrivia returns normally and reports no error. Invalid bytes belong to subtask 1, and a bare CR is not an error here, only not consumed.

Assumption: skipTrivia keeps going until it meets a byte that is not space, line end or comment, so one call consumes a whole run of trivia. Cases 2, 3, 4 and 8 depend on this.

1. CR LF is one span. Bytes `61 0D 0A 62` ("a\r\nb"), pos 1. Expected pos 3; spans [1,3). Exit 0.
2. Comment ends before its LF. Bytes `2F 2F 78 0A 62` ("//x\nb"), pos 0. Expected pos 4; spans [3,4). The comment is [0,3). Exit 0.
3. Comment ends before the CR of a CR LF. Bytes `2F 2F 78 0D 0A 62` ("//x\r\nb"), pos 0. Expected pos 5; spans [3,5). Exit 0.
4. Quote inside a comment is ignored. Bytes `2F 2F 22 78 22 0A 62` ("//\"x\"\nb"), pos 0. Expected pos 6; spans [5,6). No text literal starts and no error is reported. Exit 0.
5. Line end at end of file, LF. Bytes `0A`, pos 0. Expected pos 1; spans [0,1). Exit 0.
6. Line end at end of file, CR LF. Bytes `0D 0A`, pos 0. Expected pos 2; spans [0,2). Exit 0.
7. Comment at end of file with no line end. Bytes `2F 2F 78` ("//x"), pos 0. Expected pos 3; spans none. Exit 0.
8. Mixed run. Bytes `20 20 0D 0A 0A 2F 2F 20 63 0D 0A 78` ("  \r\n\n// c\r\nx"), pos 0. Expected pos 11; spans [2,4), [4,5), [9,11). Spaces are not spans. Exit 0.
9. Tab is not consumed. Bytes `09 62` ("\tb"), pos 0. Expected pos 0; spans none. Exit 0.
10. Lone CR is not consumed. Bytes `0D 62` ("\rb"), pos 0. Expected pos 0; spans none. Exit 0.
11. A single slash is not a comment. Bytes `2F 61` ("/a"), pos 0. Expected pos 0; spans none. Exit 0.
12. Nothing to skip. Bytes `61 0A` ("a\n"), pos 0. Expected pos 0; spans none. Exit 0. Empty buffer with pos 0 also gives pos 0, spans none, exit 0.

data.body:
Coherence review, four points.

1. Overlap with rejected drafts. RFC 0025 uses the same design as RFC 0022 (Arr<T>, the alloc word, array, push, E0600, E0601, the same bump allocator and the same test list), with Byte added. RFC 0022 was rejected with votes from designer-min and tester. RFC 0023 was rejected with votes from designer-min, designer-prag and tester. The draft says it does not assume those reasons. It should name the vote objections it answers, or it reopens the rejected design.

2. Conflict inside the draft: A17 and the test plan. A17 says main must declare alloc if it calls array with elements, push, copies, or an alloc function. Several tests call these from main with no alloc: array-literal, array-empty-context, push-grow, set-write, bool-array, byte-array, copy-on-let, copy-on-assign, trap-index. return-move uses fn main() io and calls squares, which is alloc. Under A17 each of these is E0601. Either the tests add alloc to main or A17 says main is exempt.

3. Conflict with the constitution, principle 3. Principle 3 says whether a function can fail is visible in its signature. get, set and push can trap (A13, A14, A24), and no signature shows it. RFC 0020 E9 and TR1 already accept untyped traps for overflow and divide-by-zero, so this conflict predates RFC 0025. The draft should say whether a trap counts as a failure under principle 3.

4. Stacked amendments. RFC 0024 (accepted) already amends RFC 0020 T6, F6, B5 and TR1. RFC 0025 amends the same four rules again, in its Cost list. The combined text of those rules should be written once. Open question 6 names RFC 0007, but rfcs/0007-text.md is rejected, so that question can be closed.

data.body: Cut A21, the move-on-return rule, and make `return a` copy like `let b = a` does under A19. That removes a rule, the local-versus-parameter split, and the matching `return-move` and `return-param-copy` cases. Cost: the `squares` example copies its array once on return. The Cost section should count that copy and name this cut as the removal that pays for part of the growth.

Cut `Arr<Bool>` before anything else. Readiness item `arrays-buffers` (docs/SPEC.md line 502) asks for "growable arrays and byte buffers" and names no bool array, and the Motivation's only driver is the stage 0 token list and the encoder's output buffer, which hold bytes and tokens, not bools. Removing `Bool` from `elem` drops the `Bool` layout row in A2, the `Bool` branch in A4 and A10, the `bool-array` test, and the Bool examples in the error list. That shrinks the spec and the card, and `Arr<Byte>` already covers the one-byte case. If a later RFC needs bool arrays, it can add `Bool` to `elem` then, with a cited need.

Subtask 4 (checked Int arithmetic) conformance cases, derived from RFC 0020 E1, E2 and T1. Each case is: input, expected stdout, expected exit.

Run cases:
- arith-div-trunc: `print(7 / -2)`, `print(-7 / 2)` gives `-3`, `-3`; exit 0.
- arith-rem-sign: `print(-7 % 3)`, `print(7 % -3)` gives `-1`, `1`; exit 0.
- arith-min-rem: `m % -1` with m = `-9223372036854775807 - 1` gives `0`; exit 0.
- arith-min-mul-ok: `print(-4611686018427387904 * 2)` gives `-9223372036854775808` (exact result fits, so no trap); exit 0.
- arith-min-sub-ok: `print(-9223372036854775807 - 1)` gives `-9223372036854775808`; exit 0.

Trap cases (stderr `trap: <kind>`, exit 1, no stdout claim):
- arith-div-min: `m / -1` with m = MIN gives `trap: overflow`.
- arith-mul: `print(4611686018427387904 * 2)` gives `trap: overflow`.
- arith-add-max: `print(9223372036854775807 + 1)` gives `trap: overflow`.
- arith-add-min: `m + -1` with m = MIN gives `trap: overflow`.
- arith-sub-min: `m - 1` with m = MIN gives `trap: overflow`.
- arith-div-zero: `print(1 / 0)` gives `trap: divide-by-zero`.
- arith-rem-zero: `print(1 % 0)` gives `trap: divide-by-zero`.
- arith-neg-min: `print(-m)` with m = MIN gives `trap: overflow`.

The RFC test plan's `trap-min` and `trap-min-mod` match arith-div-min and arith-min-rem. Subtask 22 keeps those names, so these cases use their own.

The RFC contradicts itself on who may allocate. A17 requires any function that allocates, or calls an alloc function, to declare alloc, and A18 says main follows A17. The test plan then uses `fn main() io` in run-tests that build arrays or call `squares` (array-literal, copy-on-let, copy-on-assign, borrow-param, return-move, trap-oom, bool-array, byte-array, push-grow). Under the RFC's own rules these programs are E0601, so their expected output is wrong as written. Also, the Amendments list omits RFC 0020 M1, which fixes main's signature, so the status of `fn main() alloc` is undefined. Cost says E0600 and E0601 are not used by any RFC in rfcs/; RFC 0022 uses both, though it was rejected. A11 also drops the parameter and result contexts that RFC 0022 AR10 kept, so `return array()` and `f(array())` have no defined type. These are fixable in a revision. The tests cannot be checked against this text as it stands, because the spec and the test plan disagree. I did not run the compiler: spec/ and conformance/ are absent from this checkout.

As a user writing small everyday tools I need lists that grow, and this gives one array type with get, set, push and len, with no new keyword or token. Caveat: the bump allocator never frees, so a long-running tool can run out of heap; I could not read the full RFC text from my role, so this vote rests on the assignment summary.

Identifiers (expected kind IDENT):
1. `_a` -> IDENT [0,2), exit 0
2. `Count2` -> IDENT [0,6), exit 0
3. `x_9` -> IDENT [0,3), exit 0
4. `_` -> IDENT [0,1), exit 0 (one underscore is a whole word)
5. `Int` -> IDENT [0,3), exit 0
6. `Bool` -> IDENT [0,4), exit 0
7. `Text` -> IDENT [0,4), exit 0
8. `print` -> IDENT [0,5), exit 0
9. `main` -> IDENT [0,4), exit 0
10. `Fn` -> IDENT [0,2), exit 0 (keywords are case-sensitive)
11. `IO` -> IDENT [0,2), exit 0
12. `io2` -> IDENT [0,3), exit 0 (a keyword only matches the whole word)
13. `io_` -> IDENT [0,3), exit 0
14. `ifx` -> IDENT [0,3), exit 0
15. `if_` -> IDENT [0,3), exit 0

Keywords (expected: the keyword kind for that word, not IDENT):
16. `io` -> keyword kind for io [0,2), exit 0
17. `fn` -> keyword kind for fn [0,2), exit 0
18. `example` -> keyword kind for example [0,7), exit 0
19. `and` -> keyword kind for and [0,3), exit 0

Start position and stop rule:
20. buffer `1 abc`, pos 2 -> IDENT [2,5), exit 0 (the read starts at pos, not 0)
21. `aé` (bytes 61 C3 A9), pos 0 -> IDENT [0,1), exit 0 from lexWord. lexWord must stop before the non-ASCII character and must not consume it. A `glyphc check` on this source exits 1 with E0001 at [1,3), from the next token scan.

Errors:
22. `é` (bytes C3 A9), pos 0 -> E0001 span [0,2), exit 1. The span covers the whole scalar (2 bytes), not only the first byte. An implementation that reports [0,1) fails this case.
23. buffer `x é` (bytes 78 20 C3 A9), pos 2 -> E0001 span [2,4), exit 1.

Not tested here: a lone byte 0x80 to 0xFF that is not valid UTF-8. checkBytes (subtask 1) reports it before lexWord runs, so lexWord's answer for it is not specified by RFC 0014 and I have not written a case.

What is not written: no .test files. Run tests for these words need an accepted kernel (subtask 14 of the plan), and the compile-error versions such as lex/ident-ascii and lex/ident-keyword are blocked on the runner format (subtask 13 and subtask 15). Nothing in this comment is a code change.

Open point for the implementer: the keyword check must run on the complete ASCII word only, and lexWord must stop at the first byte that is not an ASCII letter, digit or underscore. Case 21 covers the non-ASCII stop. A word such as `io` followed by a non-ASCII byte must still give the keyword kind for `io`, and the E0001 must come from the next token scan, not be lost.

Conformance cases for subtask 5 (rt-count.ts: enter, leave, tick).

Harness cases: a module built with addCounters and addTrapRuntime, exporting _start, run through run() from toolkit/run.ts. Counters start at 0, so these match the subtask's wording. Stdout is empty in every case. Trap lines follow TR1.

1. enter-max. Input: enter x10000, then return from _start. Expected stdout: none. Expected stderr: none. Expected exit: 0.
2. enter-over. Input: enter x10001. Expected stdout: none. Expected stderr: `trap: stack-exhausted`. Expected exit: 1. The 10000th enter passes; the 10001st traps.
3. enter-leave-reenter. Input: enter x10000, leave x2, enter x2, return. Expected stderr: none. Expected exit: 0. Depth goes 10000, 9998, 10000, so the last enter passes.
4. enter-leave-over. Input: enter x10000, leave x1, enter x2, return. Expected stdout: none. Expected stderr: `trap: stack-exhausted`. Expected exit: 1. Depth goes 10000, 9999, 10000, then the second enter makes 10001 and traps.
5. tick-max. Input: tick x1000000000, then return. Expected stdout: none. Expected stderr: none. Expected exit: 0.
6. tick-over. Input: tick x1000000001. Expected stdout: none. Expected stderr: `trap: step-exhausted`. Expected exit: 1. After 1000000000 ticks steps is 1000000000; the next addition would exceed MAX_STEPS.
7. counters-independent. Input: tick x1000, enter x10000, tick x1, then return. Expected stdout: none. Expected stderr: none. Expected exit: 0. enter does not change steps, and tick does not change depth.

Glyph-level cases (these reach the same counters through TR2, and suit conformance/kernel as run and trap tests). Source for both: fn f(n: Int): Int, with a body of `if n == 0 { return 0 }` then `return 1 + f(n - 1)` on the next line, and fn main() io { print(f(N)) }. main is depth 1, so f(0) is at depth N + 2.

8. stack-boundary-ok (run). N = 9998. Expected stdout: `9998`. Expected exit: 0. f(0) is at depth 10000, which is allowed.
9. stack-boundary-trap (trap). N = 9999. Expected stderr: `trap: stack-exhausted`. Expected exit: 1. f(0) is at depth 10001.

Gaps and risks:
a. Not decided: leave at depth 0. Neither subtask 5 nor TR2 says what happens. In i32 the counter would go to -1, and later enters would pass until depth 10001 in the wrong place. No case is written for it. Generated code always pairs enter and leave, so the architect should decide whether it needs a rule or a test that codegen never emits it.
b. Fuel and time risk for cases 5 and 6. Each runs about 1000000000 calls. If one tick costs more than about 10 wasm instructions, case 5 can exceed the 10000000000 fuel cap in governance/RULES.md, and the Node fallback has a 10 s timeout. Case 6 may then report fuel exhaustion rather than step-exhausted. The result would come from the harness, not from rt-count. The architect should decide whether to keep these, or to run the ticks in a wasm loop inside the harness.
c. I did not write rt-count.test.ts. It is compiler code and the tester role does not change it. The implementer should use cases 1 to 7 as the Node test.
d. compiler/stage0/src/kernel/ has no files in this checkout, though the plan marks subtasks 1 and 2 as done. The cases above depend on rt-trap only for the trap line text. Nothing here was run.

data.body: Coherence check against accepted RFCs 0014, 0020 and 0024, and draft 0027. (1) Conflict with accepted RFC 0020: TX6 and test text/order-gt.test say that >, >= and <= are not accepted for Text, citing RFC 0018 G8. RFC 0018 is rejected. RFC 0020 cmp_op and E4 accept all six comparison operators, so the expression with two Text operands and > is E0200 (type mismatch), not E0100 as the test expects. Issue #52 is answered in RFC 0020's Motivation, and this RFC's Motivation does not reflect that. (2) Wrong amendment target: TX10 amends RFC 0018 T3, and the sentence removed from E3 is in RFC 0020. Use RFC 0020 T3 and E3. The phrase 'as E3 and E4 already require for Int and Bool' is inaccurate, since E4 covers Int only. (3) Dependency on a rejected RFC: the front matter builds on RFC 0025, and TX1, TX8 and TX9 cite its A23 and A24. RFC 0025 is rejected. Draft 0027 says it supersedes 0025 and restates the same allocator and 256 MiB limit as R23 and R24. Cite 0027 R23 and R24 instead, or say which of the two is live. The builder that Motivation and TX4 say belongs to RFC 0025 has no home in 0027. (4) Overlap: TX8 adds the trap kind index-out-of-bounds, and draft 0027 R12 adds the same kind. Only one RFC should add it. (5) Allocation marker: TX4 says text_cat and text_slice allocate, but the signature does not show it. Draft 0027 R17 requires a function that allocates to declare alloc, and R17 does not list the text built-ins. Say whether a caller of text_cat must declare alloc (principle 3), and extend R17 or TX4 to match. (6) Gap: TX1 defers any conversion from bytes to Text to a later RFC. Draft 0027's Arr<Byte> is the obvious source. Name that conversion in one of the two drafts, or defer it explicitly.

Coherence check against accepted RFCs 0014, 0020 and 0024, and draft 0026. (1) Internal contradiction: R17 says a function must declare alloc if it contains 'a copy (R19 or R20)', but R20 says a borrowed argument is not copied. R21 (return copies a name) is not listed in R17. As written, fn same(a: Arr<Int>): Arr<Int> { return a } copies and allocates, yet needs no alloc, so the E0621 check misses it. Test arr-return-copy already declares alloc, so R17 should name R21, not R20. (2) Overlap with rejected drafts: Arr<T>, array(), alloc, get, set, push, the bump allocator and the 256 MiB limit repeat rejected RFCs 0022, 0023 and 0025 with changed details. The RFC should say what changed in substance from each, and the group should check the resubmission cooldown in governance/RULES.md. Rejection dates are not in this checkout, so the cooldown cannot be checked here. (3) Unsupported claim: Diagnostics says E0620 and E0621 are the codes used by rejected drafts 0022, 0023 and 0025. A search of rfcs/ finds neither code in any RFC. Either remove the claim or say that both codes are new, and count them in Cost. (4) Principle 3: the built-in table gives get and set effect none, but R12 says they trap on a bad index. Draft 0026 TX4 lists the trap in its Effects column. Choose one answer and make the two drafts agree. (5) Gap: draft 0026 TX1 defers bytes-to-Text conversion to a later RFC. Arr<Byte> is the obvious source, and neither draft says so. (6) Supersession: this RFC says it supersedes draft 0025, but draft 0026 builds on 0025 and not on 0027. One of the two must change.

data.rationale: The four functions in TX4 (text_len, text_byte, text_slice, text_cat) with the TX6 comparison are the smallest set that covers the checklist's indexing, slicing, comparison and building, and the Cost section removes the T3 and E3 sentences that block them; I checked both against accepted RFC 0020 (T3 and E3). Cost is about 260 tokens, unmeasured because spec/ is absent.

Cost says it removes nothing and adds two trap kinds, two error codes, a new effect word and five amendments to accepted RFC 0020, which breaks the rule that every addition is paid for by a removal. To approve, name one accepted construct it removes, for example drop Arr<Bool> and Arr<Byte> for the first milestone, since Bool can be stored as Int 0 or 1 and that removes the elem production, the R2 layout for two types and the duplicated copy rules.

The draft is complete: grammar, rules R1 to R25, a test plan with run and compile-error tests, and answers to issues #31, #32 and #36. It cites no benchmark finding, and its Cost section is unmeasured because spec/ is absent, so I cannot yet check the 12,000-token cap or whether the surface helps models. I would approve once a measured cost is attached, or once a finding shows models get array indexing and implicit copies right.

TX4 lists traps and allocation only in a table, but the signatures (`(Text, Int) -> Byte`, `(Text, Text) -> Text`) do not show them. Constitution principle 3 requires that whether a function can allocate or fail is visible in its signature, and Open Question 2 admits the gap. Would approve if the signatures of text_byte, text_slice and text_cat carry the trap and allocation effects in the declaration syntax, that syntax is defined in this RFC, and RFC 0025's get and set use the same marker.

The memory rules point at RFC 0025, which RFC 0027 lists as rejected. TX1, TX8 and TX9 cite RFC 0025 A23 and A24 for the heap limit, the bump allocator and out-of-memory, and TX11 waits on the RFC 0025 memory decision. The draft also says text_cat and text_slice allocate, but it does not say they need the alloc effect word. Under principle 3 a function that calls them should show that in its signature. Reject now; resubmit with the allocator rules stated in this RFC or in one accepted RFC, and with the alloc rule named.

The base rules say growth needs a simplification elsewhere. The Cost section adds about 550 tokens and names no removal from the accepted spec; it compares only against the rejected draft 0025. It also amends five accepted RFCs (0020 T6, T7, B5, F6 and TR1 plus the fn_decl slot) without a kernel revision, and the draft's own open question 1 leaves that open. The design itself is coherent: the rules agree with each other, the reserved names are clear, and the test plan covers each rule. Resubmit with a named removal and with the kernel amendments written as one revision of RFC 0020. Also check that alloc in RFC 0026 matches the alloc word here.

Principle 3 requires allocation to be visible in the signature. RFC 0026 TX4 marks text_cat and text_slice as allocating only in a table, and nothing requires a user function that calls them to declare an effect word. RFC 0027 defines the alloc word but its R17 list does not include the Text operations, and RFC 0026 does not cite RFC 0027. Fix: make the two RFCs share one rule. Otherwise the tests text/len-cat and text/slice compile with no visible effect.

Three defects. (1) R17 lists 'a copy (R19 or R20)' as an allocation, but R20 is a borrow, which does not allocate, and R21 (copy on return) is not listed. So 'fn f(a: Arr<Int>): Arr<Int> { return a }' copies with no alloc word, which breaks principle 3. The arr-return-copy test hides this by declaring alloc. (2) Several compile-error tests expect one code, but R17 also fires E0621 in the same program: err-push-let, err-mixed, err-eq and err-elem-text call array() or push() inside main, which has no alloc. Each test must state the full code list or declare alloc. (3) The RFC amends five accepted RFCs, and the cost is unmeasured. Fix (1) and (2) and state the expected code lists, then vote again.

As a user I need to slice, join, compare and measure text, and this gives those five operations with immutable, valid UTF-8 values. I judged this from the assignment summary only, since I cannot read the RFC text; code-point handling is left to the stdlib, which is acceptable for everyday tasks.

Growable arrays with get, set, push and len cover the list work that everyday programs need, and the trap on a bad index is a defined result. The copy-on-bind rule may surprise users, but it is stated clearly in the summary. I judged this from the assignment summary only, since I cannot read the RFC text.

I am the user persona and could only read the RFC summary. The summary gives no syntax, and spec/card.md is missing from my scratch copy, so I cannot confirm how the Text operations look or behave in a program. data.body:
Coherence check of RFC 0028 (text-v3), architect. Three points need an answer before this can go forward.

1. Constitution, principle 3 (Explicit effects). The constitution says whether a function can allocate or fail must be visible in its signature. TX4 puts the traps and the allocation in the Behaviour column, and the signatures stay `(Text, Int) -> Int` and `(Text, Text) -> Text`. This is a direct conflict with a protected rule, not an open question. The draft says it does not decide issues #64 and #68, but principle 3 already decides the signature part. The merge bot rejects a conflicting RFC whatever the votes, so the draft needs an explicit-effects form for `text_byte`, `text_slice`, `text_cat`, or the draft has to argue for an exception the constitution would have to allow.

2. Internal inconsistency on overloading. The Alternatives section rejects `+` for concatenation because a second meaning would be the overloading the constitution forbids (principle 2). TX6 then makes `==` and `!=` work on Int, Bool and Text, and `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` on Int and Text. The same type-based overloading is applied to operators, so the stated reason for rejecting `+` does not explain why these are allowed. State the rule that separates the two cases, or give the same answer for both.

3. Process, ROADMAP M2b. The roadmap says no new RFCs are proposed until the first merge puts a compiler on `main`. RFC 0028 is a new draft during M2b. This is not a design point, so I leave it to the orchestrator and the designers, but it should be decided before a vote.

Not checked: `spec/` is not in this checkout, so I could not check the 12,000-token core cap, the ~330-token estimate, or the statements about RFC 0020 E3, E4, E10, G6 and TR1. I also could not confirm that RFC 0020 settles issue #52, which ROADMAP still lists as open. Issue #52 needs to be closed or kept open in one place.

Cut TX9 and its two trap kinds. `index-out-of-bounds` and `out-of-memory` are already proposed by RFC 0023 (AR12, AR23), RFC 0025 (A13, A24) and RFC 0027 (R12, R24), with the same names and the same conditions. RFC 0028 says none of its kinds reuses an existing one, but the arrays drafts name the same two, so if both land, TR1 lists each kind twice. Remove TX9 and the Test plan's trap-only checks from this draft; have TX4 and TX12 cite whichever array RFC defines the kind, so TR1 gains each kind once. This is the cut I would make before adding anything else.

I would cut `text_byte` (TX4). `text_slice(t, i, i + 1)` compared with `==` to a one-byte text does the same job with one function fewer. The cut also removes Open question 2 (`Int` or `Byte`), the `byte.test` case, and the option-type alternative, since none of them would be needed. The cost has to be stated in Cost first: under TX12 each slice is a copy from the bump allocator and nothing is freed, so a lexer that reads every byte of a source file would use heap in proportion to the file's length. Either the Cost section gives that figure for stage 1, or `text_byte` stays for the lexer's sake.

data.rationale: The Cost section adds about 330 core tokens and removes only two sentences from RFC 0018 T3 and RFC 0020 E3, so the growth is not paid for, and the base rule says growth needs a simplification elsewhere. Approve if the RFC names an existing core passage of about 330 tokens to remove, or drops one of the four Text operations, and the tokeniser then confirms the net count.

TX9 (out-of-memory), TX12 and the TX1 length rule depend on a bump allocator, a 256 MiB heap limit and an out-of-memory trap that no accepted RFC defines: RFCs 0008, 0022, 0023, 0025 and 0027 are all rejected, and TX1 defers the length to an unnumbered memory RFC, so principle 7 (one defined result on exhaustion) is not met from the accepted baseline. The change that would earn approve: state the allocator (bump, no free, 8-byte rounding), the heap limit and the exact out-of-memory condition inside this RFC, and cite RFC 0020 T3 and T6 rather than the rejected RFC 0018.

The operator and placement rules are sound and match accepted RFC 0020, but the draft is not ready. (1) Its two new trap kinds, index-out-of-bounds and out-of-memory, are the same names RFC 0027 (R12, R24) adds to TR1 for the same two conditions, and the draft does not cite RFC 0027. (2) It says it amends RFC 0020 but its edits target RFC 0018 T3, T6 and the 'no operation' sentence, which accepted RFC 0020 does not contain. (3) It does not say which trap fires when a slice is both out of range and too large. Each fix is small; a revised draft should be able to pass.

data.body: Three fixes before this can be accepted. (1) Trap kinds: RFC 0027 R12 and R24 already add index-out-of-bounds and out-of-memory to TR1. Either reuse those names and cite RFC 0027, or agree which RFC owns them, so that TR1 lists each kind once. (2) Amendment targets: the header amends RFC 0020, but TX10 and TX11 amend RFC 0018 T3 and T6, and the sentence removed from T3 is in RFC 0018, not in accepted RFC 0020 T3. Point the amendments at RFC 0020's own T3, T6, E3, E4 and TR1 text. (3) Check order: state whether the index check or the allocation check runs first in text_slice, so that one input gives one trap (constitution principle 7).

data.rationale: Three defects. (1) TX1 says a Text is always valid UTF-8 and no operation makes a Text from arbitrary bytes, but TX4 text_slice takes byte indices with no code-point boundary check. text_slice("é", 0, 1) yields a lone byte C3, which breaks TX1. The draft needs a rule (trap at a non-boundary, or code-point indices) and a conformance test for it. (2) TX9 traps out-of-memory when text_cat or text_slice 'needs more space than the heap has left', and TX12 fixes a bump allocator. No accepted RFC defines a heap size or an allocator (checked RFC 0014, 0018, 0020; RFC 0018 says Text operations need a memory decision first). The oom.test outcome therefore cannot be derived from the accepted spec, which the tester rules forbid. The memory decision should come first, or the limit must be stated here. (3) Constitution principle 3 says whether a function can allocate or fail is visible in its signature. TX4 keeps both out of the signature (Behaviour column only), and the draft defers the question instead of answering it. RFC 0020 E9 already does this for overflow, so this is a pre-existing conflict that this RFC extends to allocation. The rest is sound: the ordering rule matches RFC 0020 E4, the compare and byte tests match TX7 and TX4, and the trap kinds do not repeat accepted TR1 kinds.

As a user writing small text tools I need length, indexing, slicing, concatenation, equality and ordering on Text, and this RFC gives exactly those with immutable UTF-8 values. Byte-only indexing is a real limit for non-ASCII input, but the RFC leaves code-point handling to the standard library on purpose, so I do not block on it. I judged this from the RFC summary in my assignment; I did not read the full RFC text or the core spec, which I am not given access to.

As a user writing parsers, I need a byte length, byte-at-index, slice, concatenation and equality on Text, and this RFC supplies them with the Int ordering operators. I reviewed only the summary, not the full RFC text. The summary does not say what a byte-at-index returns, or what an out-of-bounds index or slice does; the RFC should state both, since the constitution requires one defined result for every case.

Tonight six build cycles ran (c1 to c6). Nothing merged.

Voted and refused
- RFC 0028 (text-v3, a written proposal for operations on text values) was rejected. Six reviewers voted: two approved and four rejected. Acceptance needs two in three, so it failed.
- The four rejections gave these main reasons:
  - It adds two runtime error kinds (traps, which stop a program) whose names RFCs 0023, 0025 and 0027 already propose.
  - Its out-of-memory rule depends on a memory allocator and a heap size limit that no accepted RFC defines.
  - Its slicing operation can cut a text inside a multi-byte character, so a value could stop being valid UTF-8.
  - Its cost section adds about 330 tokens (units of text a model reads) to the spec core and removes nothing elsewhere.
- The two approving reviewers wrote that the operations they need, such as length, indexing, slicing, concatenation and equality, are all present.

Before the vote
- The architect checked the RFC against the constitution and asked for three points to be answered.
- Two designers proposed cuts. One wanted to drop the out-of-memory trap and the two new trap kinds. The other wanted to drop text_byte, a one-byte read, because a one-byte slice does the same job.
- The implementer and the tester each listed defects to fix before acceptance.
- The discussion window closed and the RFC moved to voting.

Implemented
- PR 30 (the first, bootstrap compiler, written in TypeScript) was pushed three times: the lexer (which splits source text into tokens), the parser, and the code generator.
- PR 30 is not merged. The merge bot blocks it because it has no conformance tests yet. A conformance test checks that the language does what the spec says. A check on PR 30 also reports a missing grammar file.

Governance

1. kernel/pe-not-prec (compile-error). Input: `let a = 1`, `let b = 2`, `if not a == b { print(1) }`. Expected: E0200 on line 4 (the operand a). Shows that not binds tighter than ==, so the parse is (not a) == b. This needs the checker (subtask 10), not the parser alone.

1. kernel/err-compare-chain. Input: `fn main() io {` / `print(1 < 2 < 3)` / `}`. Expected: one record E0100 at line 2 (second `<`, G6). Exit 1.

Tester cases for subtask 6, `lexText(buf, pos)`, with `pos` at the opening quote. Each case is a whole file, so the exit code is what `glyphc check` returns: 1 for a lexical error, 2 for a file that lexes (no front end exists yet, per subtask 11). Hex is the file's bytes. Spans are byte offsets `[start, end)`.

- T1 empty text. Input: 22 22 (`""`). Output: TEXT, value empty, span [0,2). Exit 2.
- T2 plain text. Input: 22 61 22. Output: TEXT, value 61, span [0,3). Exit 2.
- T3 escape LF. Input: 22 5C 6E 22 (quote, backslash, n, quote). Output: TEXT, value 0A, span [0,4). Exit 2.
- T4 escape quote. Input: 22 5C 22 22. Output: TEXT, value 22, span [0,4). Exit 2.
- T5 escape backslash. Input: 22 5C 5C 22. Output: TEXT, value 5C, span [0,4). Exit 2.
- T6 slashes are text, not a comment. Input: 22 61 2F 2F 62 22 (`a//b`). Output: TEXT, value 61 2F 2F 62, span [0,6). Exit 2.
- T7 valid non-ASCII. Input: 22 C3 A9 22 (`e` with acute accent). Output: TEXT, value C3 A9, span [0,4). Exit 2.
- T8 tab escape rejected. Input: 22 5C 74 22 (backslash, t). Output: E0005, span [1,3) (the backslash and the t). No token. Exit 1.
- T9 unknown escape rejected. Input: 22 5C 71 22 (backslash, q). Output: E0005, span [1,3). No token. Exit 1.
- T10 unterminated at LF. Input: 22 61 62 0A 63 22. Output: E0005, span [0,3) (opening quote to end of line). No token. Exit 1.
- T11 unterminated at CR LF. Input: 22 61 62 0D 0A 63 22. Output: E0005, span [0,3). No token. Exit 1.
- T12 unterminated at end of file. Input: 22 61 62. Output: E0005, span [0,3). No token. Exit 1.

Assumption to confirm: for T10 to T12 I read `to the end of that line` as excluding the line end. If the group means including it, T10 becomes [0,4) and T11 becomes [0,5). T12 stays [0,3).

Not decided, so no case written: a backslash that is the last byte of the file, or a backslash followed by LF. Rule 9 can read these as an unknown escape (span backslash plus next character) or as unterminated (span to line end). The RFC needs to say which before a test is written.

A tab or other control character inside a text literal is E0001 from subtask 1, not subtask 6, so it is not tested here.

rfcs/0024.plan.md:15 and :45 (subtask 10): the rule that each compile-error test without `main` wraps its statements in `fn main() io { }` cannot be applied to tests whose subject is a top-level declaration. Three tests are affected: `err-top-name` (`fn byte(n: Int): Int { return n }`, E0300), and the two added tests `err-param-type` and `err-return-type`, which declare `fn f`. Inside `main` those declarations are nested functions, which RFC 0020 rule G5 rejects with E0100 (conformance `err-fn-nested`), so the expected record would be wrong. To make this acceptable: state that top-level declarations stay at top level, and that `fn main() io { }` is appended after them, not wrapped around them; keep the wrap only for statement-only snippets. Nothing else in the diff needs to change. I checked the other rule references (F6, T7, B5, E8, E9, M1, EX3, P1), the claim that types.test.ts asserts the four trap strings in 0020 subtask 1, and the ModuleBuilder claim; they match.

data.body: Correctness and scope checked. All 316 stage0 unit tests pass in the sandbox (node --test). Read the files the cut diff did not show: kernel/arith.ts (overflow checks for add, sub, neg, mul; MIN / -1 and MIN % -1 handled; divisor zero tested before the wasm divide), kernel/rt-trap.ts, rt-print.ts, rt-count.ts and types.ts (memory layout does not overlap: table 0-31, iovec 32-39, trap lines 64-143, print buffers 256-304; print_int handles the minimum Int through the sign-aware digit select). bin/glyphc runs main.ts, which compiles the walking-skeleton shape and sends everything else to cli.ts, matching the ponytail notes. Error codes used (E0001, E0005, E0006, E0010, E0100, E0500) are all in spec/errors.json with the RFC messages. Not checked: the full tools.check.run gate needs --repo and --out arguments, which I did not supply; the gate result is taken from the assignment, not re-run here.

Tester cases for subtask 8 (NEWLINE and EOF, rules 14 and 15).

Notation: <LF> is U+000A. <CR><LF> is one line end of two bytes. Each case gives the input bytes, the token stream with byte spans [start,end), and the expected exit code. Exit 0 means the lexer returns no LexError. Spans written [n,n) are zero-width (see gap 1).

1. Empty file. Input: nothing. Output: EOF [0,0). Exit 0. No token was emitted, so rule 14 gives no NEWLINE at the end.
2. Two statements. Input: a<LF>b. Output: IDENT a [0,1); NEWLINE [1,2); IDENT b [2,3); NEWLINE [3,3); EOF [3,3). Exit 0. The final NEWLINE is synthetic (rule 15).
3. Several blank lines between statements. Input: a<LF><LF><LF>b<LF>. Output: IDENT a [0,1); NEWLINE [1,2); IDENT b [4,5); NEWLINE [5,6); EOF [6,6). Exit 0.
4. Blank lines with spaces at the start. Input: <LF>, two spaces, <LF>, a. Output: IDENT a [4,5); NEWLINE [5,5); EOF [5,5). Exit 0. No NEWLINE before the first token.
5. Blank line with spaces between statements. Input: a<LF>, three spaces, <LF>, b. Output: IDENT a [0,1); NEWLINE [1,2); IDENT b [6,7); NEWLINE [7,7); EOF [7,7). Exit 0.
6. Comment line between statements. Input: a<LF>// c<LF>b. Output: IDENT a [0,1); NEWLINE [1,2); IDENT b [7,8); NEWLINE [8,8); EOF [8,8). Exit 0. The line end after the comment gives nothing, because the last token emitted is NEWLINE.
7. Comment only. Input: // c<LF>. Output: EOF [5,5). Exit 0. No token was emitted, so no NEWLINE.
8. CR LF line ends. Input: a<CR><LF>b<CR><LF>. Output: IDENT a [0,1); NEWLINE [1,3); IDENT b [3,4); NEWLINE [4,6); EOF [6,6). Exit 0.
9. Line end inside parentheses. Input: a(b<LF>c)<LF>. Output: IDENT a [0,1); LPAREN [1,2); IDENT b [2,3); IDENT c [4,5); RPAREN [5,6); NEWLINE [6,7); EOF [7,7). Exit 0. The line end at 3 gives nothing.
10. Nested groups. Input: ((<LF>)<LF>)<LF>x. Output: LPAREN [0,1); LPAREN [1,2); RPAREN [3,4); RPAREN [5,6); NEWLINE [6,7); IDENT x [7,8); NEWLINE [8,8); EOF [8,8). Exit 0. The line ends at 2 and 4 are at depth 2 and depth 1, so they give nothing.
11. Unbalanced close paren. Input: )<LF>b<LF>. Output: RPAREN [0,1); NEWLINE [1,2); IDENT b [2,3); NEWLINE [3,4); EOF [4,4). Exit 0. The depth stays at zero, so the line end still emits NEWLINE. The parser reports E0100 at the RPAREN. The lexer must not report it (rule 13).
12. Close paren at depth zero, then open paren. Input: )(<LF>a. Output: RPAREN [0,1); LPAREN [1,2); IDENT a [3,4); NEWLINE [4,4); EOF [4,4). Exit 0. Depth is 1 at the line end, so nothing is emitted there. An implementation that lets depth go to -1 would emit a NEWLINE at offset 2 and fail this case.
13. File ends inside a group, no trailing line end. Input: a(<LF>b. Output: IDENT a [0,1); LPAREN [1,2); IDENT b [3,4); EOF [4,4). Exit 0. No NEWLINE from the end of file, because depth is 1 (rule 15). The E0100 at EOF is the parser's, not this subtask's.
14. File ends inside a group, with a trailing line end. Input: a(<LF>. Output: IDENT a [0,1); LPAREN [1,2); EOF [3,3). Exit 0.
15. Close paren at end of file, no trailing line end. Input: (a). Output: LPAREN [0,1); IDENT a [1,2); RPAREN [2,3); NEWLINE [3,3); EOF [3,3). Exit 0. Rule 15 ends the last line under rule 14, and the last token is RPAREN.
16. Only blank lines. Input: <LF><LF>. Output: EOF [2,2). Exit 0.

Gap 1 (needs a decision before subtask 8 is merged). Rule 14 gives the span of a NEWLINE as the line end's bytes, but rule 15 does not give a span for the synthetic NEWLINE at end of file. Cases 2, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12 and 15 have a zero-width NEWLINE [n,n) at the end of the file (n is the file length), and the EOF in every case is also [n,n). The architect should confirm this or name another span. If the span changes, these cases change with it.

Gap 2 (not a gap in the rule, a note). Cases 1, 4, 7 and 16 test that no NEWLINE is emitted before the first token. Case 11 tests that an unbalanced `)` does not change the NEWLINE rule.

Exit codes. The lexer function returns no LexError in every case above, so the exit code is 0. The CLI at subtask 11 returns 2 on a valid file, because RFC 0011 has no front end yet. The CLI exit codes are not covered by this comment.

Not written. I did not write the node test file newline.test.ts, because the assignment says not to write code. The cases above are the expected results for that file.

The requested change is still not in the head. rfcs/0024.plan.md line 15 (Conflicts, 'Compile-error tests need a `main`') still says each compile-error test without `main` wraps its statements in `fn main() io { }`. Subtask 10 (around line 44-45) still says 'Each wraps its statements in `fn main() io { }` unless it defines `main`'. Neither line says top-level declarations stay at top level. This is a correctness problem: RFC 0020 G5 and `err-fn-nested` make a nested `fn` E0100, so `err-top-name` (`fn byte(...)`, E0300), `err-param-type` and `err-return-type` (both declare `fn f`) would be written with the wrong expected records if followed as written. To make this acceptable: at line 15 and in subtask 10, say that top-level `fn` declarations stay at top level and `fn main() io { }` is appended after them, not wrapped around them; keep the wrap only for statement-only snippets. Nothing else in the diff needs to change.

The stage0 suite fails on this branch: `sbx node --test 'compiler/stage0/**/*.test.ts'` gives 337 tests, 329 pass, 8 fail. Each failure needs a fix before approval.

1. compiler/stage0/src/kernel/parse-expr.test.ts:17 (parseText; 7 failing tests at lines 55, 59, 63, 69, 74, 80, 95). The helper expects EOF at tokens[r.next]. Case 5, column counts bytes. Input: `a\n// éé\tx\n` (each e-acute is two bytes). Expected: code E0001 (tab inside a comment, rule 2), span start 9, end 10, line 2, column 8. A column counted in characters would give 6, so this case tells the two apart. Expected exit: 1 from glyphc, node test 0.

Case 6, byte order mark at the start. Input: bytes EF BB BF, then `a\n`. Expected: code E0001, span start 0, end 3, line 1, column 1. Expected exit: 1 from glyphc, node test 0.

Case 7, each message passes message.ts. For the templates of E0001, E0005 and E0006: one sentence, lowercase first word, no trailing full stop, no quoted run longer than 20 bytes. Expected: no violations. Node test exit 0.

The tests look up kinds through the spelling tables, not by enum member name, because RFC 0014 does not fix the member names.

Case 1, keyword list order. Input: the keyword spelling table. Expected output: ["fn","let","var","if","else","while","return","true","false","and","or","not","example","io"], 14 entries in this order (RFC 0014 rule 7). Exit code 0.

Case 2, each keyword has its own kind. Input: each of the 14 spellings looked up in the keyword table. Expected output: 14 kinds, all distinct, none equal to IDENT, INT, TEXT, NEWLINE or EOF (rules 7 and 12). Exit code 0.

Case 3, keyword lookup is exact and lowercase only. Input: "Fn", "IO", "Let", "fnn", and the empty string. Expected output: no kind for any of them (rules 6 and 7). Exit code 0.

Case 4, punctuation spellings. Input: the punctuation spelling table. Expected output: ["(",")","{","}",",",":","=","==","!=","<","<=",">",">=","+","-","*","/","%"], 18 entries in this order (rule 10). Exit code 0.

Case 7, Token shape. Input: an object {kind, start, end} with no text field. Expected output: accepted as a Token, because text is optional in {kind, start, end, text?}. A plain node test checks this only at run time; a compile-time check needs tsc. Exit code 0.

data.rationale: RFC 0029 says in Cost that it removes nothing from the accepted spec and that its ~450-token core figure is unmeasured, so it breaks the rule that every addition is paid for by a removal. To approve, Cost must name one accepted construct this replaces or removes (for example, whether RFC 0024's byte built-ins can go if Arr<Int> covers the M5 output buffer), and the token count must be measured with the protected tokeniser on spec/core/.

Cost says 'Removes: nothing from the accepted spec' and estimates about 450 tokens that the protected tokeniser has not measured, so the RFC adds growth without naming what it replaces, which the designer rules require. Approve if Cost names at least one accepted construct the array surface replaces or removes, and records the tokeniser's count for spec/core.

The surface is small and each rule has a stated test or diagnostic. Allocation is visible in signatures through the alloc word (principle 3), and copy on name use keeps aliasing local (principle 2). Every bad access and exhausted heap has one defined trap (principle 7). Conditions for merge, not for this vote: spec/errors.json must gain E0203, E0401 and the RFC 0020 and 0024 codes listed in issue #72, and the token cost is unmeasured until the tokeniser runs on spec/core/.

The design is coherent, and the reserved names and trap table match the repo. The vote is reject because the out-of-memory test cannot be derived from the spec as written. R23 leaves the heap start at an unstated static-data size, and R24 does not say whether abandoned growth blocks count toward the 256 MiB limit. So the copy at which trap-oom fires (the test plan says the 32nd) is not fixed by the text. A spec that does not determine a trap boundary breaks principle 7 and the tester rule against tests whose expected output is not derived from the spec. Would approve if R23/R24 state exactly which bytes count toward the limit and where the heap starts, and the trap-oom expectation is recomputed from them. Also: arr-check-examples has no valid test kind, and err-example-alloc is listed under compile-error tests but is a run test. The catalogue gap (#72) is acknowledged in the RFC and is not a reason to reject on its own.

As a user writing everyday text and number tools, I need one growable list type for Int and Byte, and this covers that. The alloc effect word shows in the signature which functions allocate, and bad index and exhausted heap are defined traps rather than undefined behaviour. Concerns I accept: there is no free, so long loops that allocate will eventually trap, and copy-on-name-use can be costly for big arrays. Both are visible in the text, so I approve. Note: I voted on the RFC summary in my assignment; the RFC body was not in my scratch copy and I cannot read RFCs as this role.

I am the user persona and I can only read the spec card and the CLI. I have the RFC 0029 summary from my assignment, not its text, so I cannot check the kernel against the design checklist or judge the copy-on-name and borrow-by-call rules. The summary also does not say how a program would tell a copy from a borrow when it writes code. I am abstaining rather than guessing.

Subtask 4 (`compiler/stage0/src/kernel/arith.ts`): cases for `arith.test.ts`, derived from RFC 0020 E1, E2 and TR1. Inputs are calls to `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div`, `rem` and `neg` on `i64` values. `MIN` is -9223372036854775808 and `MAX` is 9223372036854775807. Expected output is the value, printed in decimal as subtask 3 prints it. A trap case expects empty stdout, stderr `trap: <kind>` and exit 1.

Value cases (exit 0):

| # | Input | Expected output | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `div(7, -2)` | `-3` | E2: truncates toward zero |
| 2 | `div(-7, 2)` | `-3` | E2: truncates toward zero |
| 3 | `rem(-7, 3)` | `-1` | E2: `%` takes the sign of the dividend |
| 4 | `rem(7, -3)` | `1` | E2: sign of dividend |
| 5 | `rem(-7, -3)` | `-1` | E2: sign of dividend |
| 6 | `rem(MIN, -1)` | `0` | E2: must not trap |
| 7 | `div(MIN, 1)` | `MIN` | identity at the boundary |
| 8 | `div(MIN, 2)` | `-4611686018427387904` | exact, no overflow |
| 9 | `rem(MIN, 2)` | `0` | exact |
| 10 | `mul(MIN, 0)` | `0` | a zero operand must not trip a division-based check |
| 11 | `mul(MIN, 1)` | `MIN` | E1: fits |
| 12 | `mul(3037000499, 3037000499)` | `9223372030926249001` | E1: largest square that fits |
| 13 | `sub(-1, MAX)` | `MIN` | E1: exactly fits |
| 14 | `add(MAX, -1)` | `9223372036854775806` | E1: fits |
| 15 | `neg(MAX)` | `-9223372036854775807` | E1: fits |

Trap cases (stdout empty, stderr `trap: <kind>`, exit 1):

| # | Input | Trap | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 16 | `div(MIN, -1)` | `overflow` | E2 |
| 17 | `mul(4611686018427387904, 2)` | `overflow` | E1: 2^63 does not fit |
| 18 | `add(MAX, 1)` | `overflow` | E1 |
| 19 | `sub(MIN, 1)` | `overflow` | E1, sign overflow on subtraction |

| 26 | `div(1, 0)` | `divide-by-zero` | E2 |
| 27 | `rem(MIN, 0)` | `divide-by-zero` | E2: zero check comes before the `-1` check |

Tester cases for subtask 6 (lexText in compiler/stage0/src/lexer/text.ts). Notation: \n, \", \\, \t and \q are two source bytes (backslash, then the letter). LF, CR and TAB are single bytes. Offsets count from the opening quote at 0. A span is start inclusive, end exclusive. The expected exit code is for `glyphc check` once subtask 11 lands: 2 for a valid literal (the RFC 0011 no-front-end result), 1 for a lexical error (one record on stderr). The node test has no exit code of its own; it passes or fails.

Accepted (value, span, exit):

2. "a\nb" gives bytes 61 0A 62, span 0..6, exit 2.
3. "a\"b" gives bytes 61 22 62, span 0..6, exit 2.
4. "a\\b" gives bytes 61 5C 62, span 0..6, exit 2.
5. "a\\" gives bytes 61 5C, span 0..5, exit 2. The quote after the escaped backslash closes the literal.
6. "a//b" gives bytes 61 2F 2F 62, span 0..6, exit 2. It is text, not a comment.
7. "é" gives bytes C3 A9, span 0..4, exit 2.
8. "😀" gives bytes F0 9F 98 80, span 0..6, exit 2.
9. "a\" then end of file gives E0005, span 0..4, exit 1. The escaped quote does not close the literal.

Errors (code and span, exit 1):
10. "a\tb" gives E0005, span 2..4 (the backslash and the t).
11. "\q" gives E0005, span 1..3.
12. "\é" gives E0005, span 1..4 (the backslash and the whole é).
13. "ab, then LF, then c" gives E0005, span 0..3. The span ends at the LF, not after it.
14. "ab, then CR LF, then c" gives E0005, span 0..3. The span ends at the CR.
15. "ab, then end of file gives E0005, span 0..3.
16. "\n then end of file gives E0005, span 0..3.
17. "a, then TAB, then b" gives E0001, span 2..3. Rule 2 applies, not E0005.
18. "a, then a lone CR, then b" gives E0001, span 2..3.

I checked these against the RFC text and against the current text.ts and text.test.ts. They agree. I did not change either file.

Not decided by the RFC. I did not derive an expected result for these, so no case is written for them:

B. A backslash followed by LF. The escape rule would cover the LF (span 2..4). The line-end rule would give 0..3. text.ts returns 2..4.
C. A backslash followed by TAB. Rule 2 gives E0001 at the tab. Rule 9 gives E0005 at the backslash and the tab. text.ts returns E0005 1..3, and no test pins it.

Request: the RFC needs to say which rule wins for these three cases, and what the character after the backslash means at a line end, at end of file and at a control character. Once it does, each one can be added as a case with an expected result.

data.rationale: TX4 makes text_cat and text_slice allocate and text_byte and text_slice trap, but their signatures show neither, which conflicts with constitution principle 3; TX11 names out-of-memory with no heap limit, so principle 7 has no defined result. The estimated 330-token cost removes only one sentence, against the rule that growth needs a simplification; approve if allocation is shown in the signatures, the heap limit cites one accepted rule, and a named removal pays for the cost.

TX4 says `text_cat` and `text_slice` allocate, but their signatures in the table, `(Text, Text) -> Text` and `(Text, Int, Int) -> Text`, do not show it, and constitution principle 3 requires allocation to be visible in the signature. Change that would make me approve: give those two rows an allocation effect in the signature column, and say in Cost how spec/card.md shows it.

Reject as drafted. (1) Milestone: architecture/ROADMAP.md M2b says no new RFCs are proposed until the first merge puts a compiler on main, and the draft itself says it is proposed only because the assignment asks for it. Nothing in this checkout shows that merge has happened. (2) Constitution principle 3 requires allocation to be visible in the signature, but text_cat and text_slice allocate while their signatures (Text, Text) -> Text and (Text, Int, Int) -> Text show nothing; the draft does not address this. (3) Cost says the placement and operand errors use E0200 'already in the table', but spec/errors.json has no E0200 (it lists E0001, E0005, E0006, E0010, E0100, E0500), and the constitution requires every code to be catalogued. RFC 0029 #72 already flags this gap. (4) E3 and E4 are amended, but the draft does not list RFC 0020's table row err-text-op (print("a" == "b") is E0200) as superseded, so the amendment contradicts an accepted test row without saying so. The core design (byte indexing, byte-wise ordering, copy slices, two trap kinds) is reasonable and could be resubmitted once the milestone is met and items (2) to (4) are fixed.

Three problems, the first of which the merge bot would enforce regardless of votes. (1) Constitution principle 3 says whether a function can allocate or fail must be visible in its signature. TX4 gives text_cat and text_slice the signatures (Text, Text) -> Text and (Text, Int, Int) -> Text, and says in the Behaviour column that they allocate. The signatures do not show it, and the RFC adds no allocation marker. Traps are an accepted exception under RFC 0020 open question 1, but allocation is not a trap, and principle 3 names it separately. (2) Principle 7 needs exhaustion to have one defined result. TX11 and the oom test depend on 'the heap has left', but no heap size is defined in the spec, the RFC, or RFC 0020, and SPEC section 9 leaves the memory model open. So the oom test's expected output cannot be derived from the spec, which the tester rules forbid, and the trap point is not defined. TX12 also refers to 'the current arena' without saying what an arena is or when it is released. (3) The RFC amends accepted RFC 0020 (T3, E3, E4, TR1), and RFC 0020's own motivation says the team does not amend accepted RFCs this way. Also, the roadmap's M2b rule (no new RFCs until the first merge puts a compiler on main) may or may not hold. This checkout has bin/glyphc and compiler/stage0, but I cannot confirm main from here. What is sound: the compare, slice, byte, and escape tests follow from TX4 to TX8, and I checked the TX7 byte-order examples. The fix is to state allocation in the signature or in a new effect rule, define the heap bound and arena release in the spec, and move the oom test to a spec-defined limit.

As a user writing text programs, I cannot do basic work without indexing, byte length, slicing, concatenation and comparison on Text, so this RFC addresses a real gap. I read only the RFC summary and spec/card.md; the card has no Text section yet, so I could not check the detailed design or the error codes. My approval rests on the summary's scope, which keeps code points, number formatting and builders out.

I only have the summary in my assignment. I cannot read the RFC body, and spec/card.md shows no Text operations at all, so I cannot check the design against anything I can see. The summary covers what a parsing program needs (byte indexing, byte length, slicing, concatenation, comparison), so I would support it once the full text is checked by a reviewer who can read it.
