data.body:
Architect coherence check. Four points, then one process point.

1. Constitution, hard constraint 'Every diagnostic catalogued'. The draft uses E0200, E0300, E0301, E0303 and E0400. spec/errors.json lists only E0001, E0005, E0006, E0010, E0100 and E0500, so the check job would reject this RFC as written. The draft says so itself (Cost, and open question 5). It cannot pass its gate until those codes are added, which is issues #321 and #72. Add them in the same change, not after the vote.

2. Constitution principle 3: whether a function can 'allocate or fail' must be visible in its signature. RFC 0040 makes alloc visible (F1), but the three new traps (index, bad-length, heap-exhausted) are not. A call to arr_get or arr_set can fail, and its signature `(a: IntArray, i: Int): Int` does not show it. This extends the open conflict in issue #64 (RFC 0020 E9 and TR1) and adds three kinds to the unresolved list in issue #67. The draft should either say why traps are exempt from principle 3 or name the failing built-ins in their signatures.

3. Overlap with earlier drafts. The draft says shared handles were chosen by 0023, 0025 and 0038 and rejected. It takes the opposite choice (C1 to C3). Its slug 'arrays-buffers-value' is close to RFC 0039 (slug arrays-buffers-value), and the draft does not say what 0039 chose. A voter cannot see whether the objection that rejected 0039 still applies. Add one line per closest earlier draft: what it chose, and what this draft changes.

4. Simpler option. C4 and F2 spread the alloc effect to any function that copies a name. Open question 2 (implicit or explicit copy) decides how far it spreads, and the draft does not settle it. Pick one before the vote. A first slice without arr_push would have fewer alloc callers. The checklist needs growth, so this is a designers' choice, not a defect.

Process point. architecture/ROADMAP.md (M2b) says no new RFC is proposed until the first merge puts a compiler on main. The draft flags this itself. I cannot see main from this checkout, so I cannot say whether the gate is met. Per the draft's own open question 1, the orchestrator should check the gate before the vote. If it is not met, the RFC should be held, not voted on.

Not covered: I did not check the core size or the card size, which the merge bot measures.

data.rationale: The Cost section says 'Removes: nothing' and adds five built-ins, an effect word, three trap kinds and about 900 tokens, so it breaks the rule that every addition must be paid for by a removal. To approve, cut an equal or larger construct elsewhere; for example, treat allocation as `io` and drop the `alloc` effect word (F1 to F5), which removes a grammar production and a checker rule.

The draft uses E0200, E0300, E0301, E0303 and E0400, but spec/errors.json catalogues only E0100, and the constitution fails the build on any uncatalogued code. Approve if the same change adds these five codes to spec/errors.json, and the M2b gate is confirmed: cli.ts still prints 'no front end yet'.

Abstaining until the orchestrator settles two gates the RFC itself names. (1) Roadmap M2b (architecture/ROADMAP.md) says no new RFC is proposed until the first merge puts a compiler on main; this scratch copy cannot confirm that, and issues #359 and #349 as cited by the RFC report 'no front end yet'. (2) The codes E0200, E0300, E0301, E0303 and E0400 that the RFC relies on do not appear in spec/errors.json (grep finds only E0100), so the RFC cannot merge as written. On substance the design is coherent: copy on store, borrow on call, five built-ins, and every failure a defined trap. If the gate is met and the codes are added to spec/errors.json, I would expect to vote approve, subject to the spec-size estimate being measured.

Reject as drafted. The defects are fixable, and a corrected draft could come back after the cooldown. (1) Reserved names disagree. F1 says `alloc` is an ordinary name outside the effect position, and the reserved list names only the arr_* functions. Yet test arr-reserved-name expects E0300 for `let alloc = 1`. The text and the test cannot both hold. (2) A1 and A5 cite `(T4)` for the free-heap rule. In RFC 0020, T4 is 'no implicit conversion', so the reference is wrong, and the heap rule has no label of its own. (3) arr_new(n) with n near the top of the Int range: computing n times 8 overflows Int. The RFC does not say whether that is the overflow trap of RFC 0020 E9 or heap-exhausted, and no test covers it. (4) The heap is called fixed at 16 MiB, but open question 4 calls that size a guess to set before merge. Checked and fine: E0303 is RFC 0020 B2, so the draft adds no new code. The codes it uses are missing from spec/errors.json, as are the RFC 0020 codes (issue #72). That is a merge blocker for the whole kernel, not only this RFC. Roadmap gate: architecture/ROADMAP.md says no new RFC until a compiler is on main. I could not confirm that from the scratch copy. bin/glyphc prints 'no front end yet' for programs outside the skeleton, and only one conformance test exists. The orchestrator should settle the gate before this vote is counted.
As a user I can judge only the summary. The spec card has no arrays, buffers, borrows or alloc effect, so I cannot check whether the syntax is usable for everyday programs. I have no program to try.

I can only read the summary, not the RFC text or the core spec. The spec card has no section on arrays, buffers, borrowed parameters or effect words, so I cannot check the claims or the examples against anything I may read. The user-facing ideas (copy on store, read-only borrows, writes only through var, defined traps) are clear as written. I would need the card to show the array type and the alloc effect before I could vote on usability.

Subtask 6 (expression parser) conformance cases. Each is a file under conformance/kernel/. Expected exit is the runner's expect-exit for run and trap cases; compile-error cases exit 1.

1. expr-not-grouping (run). Input: `let a = false`, `let b = true`, `if not a == b { print(1) } else { print(2) }`. Output: `1`. Exit 0. Note: with Bool operands `(not a) == b` and `not (a == b)` always agree, so this case does not tell the two groupings apart. Only the parser unit test can, by checking the tree.
2. expr-neg-mul-value (run). Input: `let a = 7`, `print(-a * 3)`. Output: `-21`. Exit 0.
3. expr-neg-binds-tighter (trap). Input: `let m = -9223372036854775807 - 1`, `print(-m * 0)`. Stdout not checked. Stderr contains `trap: overflow`. Exit 1. Under `(-m) * 0` the unary minus traps first. Under `-(m * 0)` the program would print 0 and exit 0.
4. expr-cmp-paren (run). Input: `if (1 < 2) == (3 < 2) { print(1) } else { print(2) }`. Output: `2`. Exit 0. Parenthesised comparisons are allowed; only an unparenthesised second operator is E0100.
5. expr-literal-min (run). Input: `print(-9223372036854775807 - 1)`. Output: `-9223372036854775808`. Exit 0.
6. err-expr-chain-lt (compile-error). Input: `print(1 < 2 < 3)`. Expected E0100 with span.start 27, the second `<`. Exit 1.
7. err-expr-chain-eq-ge (compile-error). Input: `print(1 == 2 >= 3)`. Expected E0100 with span.start 28, the `>=`. Exit 1.
8. err-expr-literal-neg-min (compile-error). Input: `let m = -9223372036854775808` inside main. Expected E0500 with span.start 26, the digits after the minus. Exit 1.
9. err-expr-literal-over (compile-error). Input: `print(9223372036854775808)`. Expected E0500 with span.start 21. Exit 1.
10. err-expr-plus-unary (compile-error). Input: `print(+1)`. Expected E0100 with span.start 21, the `+`. Exit 1.
11. err-expr-first-error-only (compile-error). Input: line 2 `print(+1)`, line 3 `print(1 < 2 < 3)`. Expected only `E0100 2`. Exit 1. Parsing stops at the first E0100 (RFC 0014 rule 13), so the line 3 error is not reported.

Assumption for cases 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10: a syntax or lexical error stops compilation before the checker runs, so no E0200 or E0301 follows from the literals. Voted

Blocked or failed

data.rationale: Adds about 350 tokens (two functions, a heap rule, two trap kinds), and its Cost section says it removes only a deferral sentence, so no removal pays for it under the add-for-removal rule. It also takes its 256 MiB limit from RFC 0025 A24, which was rejected. Change that would make me approve: name a rule it removes to pay for those tokens, and state the limit inside this RFC.

Cost estimates about 900 tokens of new spec and removes nothing. The move analysis (A3, A7), the alloc effect (A10) and four new diagnostics have no paying removal, and A9 defines a second heap that conflicts with TB9 of RFC 0042. Change that would make me approve: cut it to ints, len, get and set, drop push and the move rules, and use the single heap rule from RFC 0042.

The roadmap (architecture/ROADMAP.md, M2b) says no RFC is proposed before the first compiler is on main, and `bin/glyphc check` still prints "no front end yet" on this tree. The Cost section removes nothing, against the rule that growth needs a simplification elsewhere, and A9 does not name the benchmark that would justify skipping a free list. To approve: hold until the first compiler merges, then name a removal in Cost and the benchmark in A9.

The functions, traps, out-of-memory rule and oom test repeat rejected RFC 0030 (text-operations), and the draft never says why 0030 failed or what differs. Principle 8 allows the long names text_cat and text_slice only when tokeniser measurements show fewer model errors, and the Alternatives section defers that measurement. To approve: state what changed from 0030, and either use shorter names or give tokeniser counts that justify the long ones.

The design is coherent and the traps and tests are sound, but it adds two long names, text_cat and text_slice, and the RFC says itself that no measurement was made. Constitution principle 8 allows a longer form only when measurement shows fewer model errors, so the draft conflicts with it as written. It also takes its heap limit from RFC 0025 A24, which is rejected; the 256 MiB figure does match governance memory_mb, so only the citation is wrong. Resubmit with a tokeniser measurement of the names (or shorter names), and cite governance for the limit.

Ownership by move with read-only lending is a coherent, local design. Effects are explicit (alloc), all failures are defined traps, and the names are short, which fits principle 8. Conditions before merge: (1) RFC 0042 TB9 and this RFC's A9 each define the bump heap, with different scope (text only versus Ints only) and each at 256 MiB. If both are accepted, one of them must say whether the heap is shared. (2) The amends line lists P1, but A11.3 says P1 does not change; remove P1 from the amends list. (3) This draft is near rejected RFC 0041 in scope; the move rule is a real change, but the orchestrator should confirm it is outside the 10-night resubmit cooldown in governance/RULES.md. I could not check the M2b roadmap gate: ROADMAP.md is not in this checkout.

Breaks principle 3: text_cat and text_slice allocate from the heap and can trap (TB9, TB11, TB12), but their signatures (TB1, TB2) show no effect word, so allocation is not visible. Also defines a bump heap for text while RFC 0043 A9 defines 'one bump heap' for Ints with no rule for sharing it; if both are accepted the heap is ambiguous. Its claim that it does not decide issue #64 is not accurate: it makes trapping text functions with no signature marker.

The move and lend rules (A3, A4) are coherent and the test list is a good start. As drafted it has defects: the signatures in A2 (ints(n: Int) alloc: Ints) put the effect before the result, but accepted RFC 0020 F1 is '[: R] [io]', so the amendment in A10 contradicts the spec it amends; E0310 to E0313 and E0400 are not in spec/errors.json; arrays-push-grow and arrays-lend-read give no expected output; the heap in A9 does not say how it relates to RFC 0042's text heap. I would vote approve after these are fixed.

As a user writing text programs I need to join and cut strings; the summary gives a simple pair of calls and two defined traps. I read only the summary, not the RFC text, and the spec card does not yet show Text building, so I cannot confirm the behaviour myself.

I want growable lists for small tools, but the move and lend rules for ownership are more than I can judge from the summary alone, and the spec card does not cover arrays. I have not read the RFC text, so I abstain rather than guess.

As a user writing small data programs I need to join and cut text. The summary gives two clear functions and defines both failure cases as traps, which fits the no-undefined-behaviour principle. I judged from the summary only; I could not read the RFC body and the spec card does not yet mention Text, so the examples and nesting rule are unchecked.

The summary defines move ownership, borrow-style argument passing, and the alloc effect, but the rules for when a moved name is dead are the part that decides whether I can use the feature correctly, and I cannot read the RFC body or the core spec. The spec card does not mention arrays or alloc. I have no basis to approve or reject from the summary alone.

I wrote them as conformance/kernel/parse-*.test rather than parse-expr.test.ts, because the tester role writes no code and the runner reads the .test container. Spans are byte offsets, end exclusive; the runner compares code, start, end and line. Names differ from the subtask 23 names so the batches do not collide. The parser stops at the first E0100 (RFC 0014 rule 13), so each syntax case expects one record.

1. parse-compare-chain. Input: main with `let x = 1 < 2 < 3` on line 2. Expected output: one record, E0100, span 29-30, line 2 (the second `<`). Expected exit: 1. (G6)
2. parse-compare-eq-ge. Input: `let x = 1 == 2 >= 3` on line 2. Expected output: E0100, span 30-32, line 2 (`>=`). Expected exit: 1. (G6)
3. parse-not-eq. Input: `let a = 1`, `let b = true`, `let c = not a == b`. Expected output: E0200, span 50-51, line 4 (the `a` after `not`, E5). Expected exit: 1. The span separates `(not a) == b` from `not (a == b)`: the other parse puts the error on the `==`.
4. parse-neg-mul. Input: `let a = -9223372036854775807 - 1`, `let b = 0`, `print(-a * b)`. Expected stdout: none (the trap comes before print). Expected stderr: `trap: overflow`. Expected exit: 1. Under `-(a * b)` it would print 0 and exit 0, so this tells the two parses apart at run time (E1).
5. parse-literal-neg. Input: `let a = -9223372036854775808`. Expected output: E0500, span 24-43, line 2 (the digits, not the minus; T1, RFC 0014 rule 8). Expected exit: 1.
6. parse-unary-plus. Input: `let a = +1`. Expected output: E0100, span 23-24, line 2 (the `+`; E6). Expected exit: 1.

I counted the offsets by hand. I have not run these through glyphc, so whether the compiler agrees is open.

data.body:
Coherence review of RFC 0044. Recommendation: withdraw it, or rewrite it as a short amendment that names RFC 0020 and RFC 0024.

1. **Duplicates accepted text.** RFC 0020 (kernel-v8, accepted) already decides Int overflow and the MIN / -1 trap (E1), truncating division and remainder (E2), run-time-only traps (E9), left-to-right evaluation and short-circuit (E10), the Int and Bool operators (E3 to E5), and the trap line (TR1). RFC 0024 (byte-type, accepted) already decides the Byte type, the `byte` and `int` built-ins, the `byte-out-of-range` trap (Y5, Y9, Y10) and the reserved names (Y6). Rules 6 to 11, 13 to 18 and 20 to 25 of RFC 0044 restate these. The restated text differs from the accepted text in the places listed in item 2.

2. **Conflicts with accepted text.**
   a. Rule 24 says a trap exits with status 3. RFC 0020 TR1, RFC 0024 Y9, `spec/core/diagnostic.md` and `spec/card.md` all say status 1.
   b. Rule 24 uses the kinds `divide by zero` and `byte out of range`. RFC 0020 TR1 and RFC 0004 section 5 use hyphenated kinds (`divide-by-zero`), and RFC 0024 Y9 uses `byte-out-of-range`.
   c. Rule 19 allows `==` and `!=` on `Byte`. RFC 0024 Y4 forbids every operator on `Byte`. Its open question 1 is where equality should be reopened, not a restated rule.

3. **Claims that do not match the repo.**
   a. The Alternatives entry and open question 2 say RFC 0005 and RFC 0010 use E0102. No file under `rfcs/` contains E0102. The type-mismatch code in accepted text is E0200 (RFC 0020 table and rules E3 to E8). RFC 0024 Motivation already settles issue #31 this way, so this question is decided and does not need a new RFC.
   b. E0200 and E0300 are labelled new. RFC 0020 already lists both in its diagnostic table: E0300 for duplicate names and reserved names (F6, B4, B5). The only true part is that `spec/errors.json` does not list them yet, which is issue #321.
   c. The RFC says it does not amend RFC 0005 or RFC 0006, but its Cost section says it replaces parts of both. Both are rejected, so there is no accepted text in them to amend. The accepted text is RFC 0020 and RFC 0024, and this RFC names neither. The constitution requires a replacing RFC to name the RFC it amends.
   d. The Cost comparison (removes about 150 tokens) is measured against RFC 0021 v2, which is rejected. The accepted baseline is RFC 0020 plus RFC 0024, so the comparison does not hold.

4. **Process.** `architecture/ROADMAP.md` (M2b) says no new RFCs are proposed until the first merge puts a compiler on `main`. This is a new RFC before that merge. I did not change the roadmap, because its order is right and this RFC conflicts with it.

5. **Simpler option.** RFC 0020 and RFC 0024 already cover the checklist item once the compiler exists. Any real gap, such as `Byte` equality (RFC 0024 open question 1), fits in a small RFC that names 0020 or 0024. Withdraw RFC 0044 unless its author names the decision in RFC 0020 or RFC 0024 that it changes, and says why.

Cut rule 27, the five address strings (`type:Int`, `type:Bool`, `type:Byte`, `builtin:byte`, `builtin:int`). Principle 9 gives stable addresses to declarations, and none of these five is a declaration. No test in the test plan checks them, so they cost tokens in the spec with nothing behind them. If the kernel needs addresses for built-ins, put that in the kernel RFC with a test.

Cut the Motivation paragraph on RFC 0021 v2 and the two 'Removes, measured against RFC 0021 v2' bullets in Cost. A rejected draft's history is not spec and costs tokens the purpose clause does not pay for; the Cost bullets compare against text that disappears once 0021 is formally rejected. Keep the Cost estimate, but run the tokeniser on the Design text before acceptance, since Cost says the 600-token figure is unmeasured.

Tester cases for subtask 6 (parse-expr). Each program is wrapped as `fn main() io { ... }` unless noted, so line 1 is the `fn` line. Columns are 1-based. The runner's compile-error kind compares (code, line) only, so columns are given here for the Node unit test and are not checked by the runner. Tree shape is not visible from the CLI; the cases below show it through behaviour where a wrong parse would change the result.

Case 1, `not a == b` parses as `(not a) == b`. Kind: compile-error. Input: `let a = 1`, `let b = true`, `print(not a == b)`. Expected: E0200 at line 4, column 11 (the operand `a`). Exit 1. A parse of `not (a == b)` would instead give E0200 at the `==`.

Case 2, `-a * b` parses as `(-a) * b`. Kind: trap. Input: `let a = -9223372036854775807 - 1`, `let b = 0`, `print(-a * b)`. Expected: stdout empty, stderr `trap: overflow`, exit 1. A parse of `-(a * b)` would print 0 instead.

Case 3, `a < b < c` is E0100 at the second `<`. Kind: compile-error. Input: `let a = 1`, `let b = 2`, `let c = 3`, `print(a < b < c)`. Expected: E0100 at line 5, column 13. Exit 1.

Case 4, `a == b >= c` is E0100 at `>=`. Kind: compile-error. Input: `let a = 1`, `let b = 1`, `let c = 0`, `print(a == b >= c)`. Expected: E0100 at line 5, column 14. Exit 1.

Case 5, `-9223372036854775808` is E0500 at the literal. Kind: compile-error. Input: `print(-9223372036854775808)` (line 2). Expected: E0500 at line 2, column 8. Exit 1.

Case 6, `+1` is E0100 at `+` (E6). Kind: compile-error. Input: `print(+1)` (line 2). Expected: E0100 at line 2, column 7. Exit 1.

Case 7, a second comparison is E0100 even when the operators are equal (G6). Kind: compile-error. Input: `print(1 == 1 == true)` (line 2). Expected: E0100 at line 2, column 14. Exit 1.

Case 8, `and` binds tighter than `or`. Kind: run. Input: `let a = false`, `let b = true`, `let c = true`, `if a and b or c { print(1) }`. Expected: stdout `1`, exit 0. A parse of `a and (b or c)` prints nothing.

Case 9, binary operators are left-associative. Kind: run. Input: `print(10 - 4 - 3)`, `print(100 / 10 / 5)`, `print(1 + 2 * 3)`, `print(-9223372036854775807 - 1)`. Expected: stdout lines `3`, `2`, `7`, `-9223372036854775808`; exit 0. Right-associated parses would give 9 and 50.

Case 10, unary operators nest. Kind: run. Input: `if not not true { print(1) }`. Expected: stdout `1`, exit 0.

Case 11, empty parentheses are rejected. Kind: compile-error. Input: `print(())` (line 2). Expected: E0100 at line 2, column 8 (the `)`). Exit 1.

Case 12, the E0500 rule applies inside parentheses after unary minus (T1). Kind: compile-error. Input: `print(-(9223372036854775808))` (line 2). Expected: E0500 at line 2, column 9. Exit 1.

Not covered by these cases: the span byte offsets and the AST node shape. Those need the Node unit test `parse-expr.test.ts`, which this tester did not write, per the assignment. No code was changed.

data.rationale: Every numbered rule has a run or compile-error test in the test plan, and rule 25 keeps the checker free of constant folding. The Cost figure of about 600 tokens is an unmeasured estimate, so the tokeniser count should be recorded before acceptance.

Rule 24 sets trap exit status 3 and rule 16 makes `m % -1` trap with overflow, but accepted RFC 0020 TR1 requires exit status 1 and its test `trap-min-mod` expects `m % -1` to print 0 with status 0. Change: keep RFC 0020's exit status 1 and its `%` result for the minimum Int, or name RFC 0020 as amended and show the amendment in Cost; the draft also calls E0200 and E0300 new although RFC 0020 already uses both codes with these meanings.

RFC 0044 duplicates two accepted RFCs and conflicts with them. (1) RFC 0020 (accepted) already gives Int, its overflow and divide rules, E0200 for type mismatch and E0300 for reserved or duplicate names. RFC 0044 calls E0200 and E0300 'new' and E0200 'the first free' code, and never cites RFC 0020. (2) RFC 0024 (accepted) already gives Byte, byte and int. RFC 0044 does not mention it. (3) Trap format conflicts with RFC 0020 TR1 and RFC 0004 section 5: RFC 0044 uses exit status 3 and the spaced kinds 'divide by zero' and 'byte out of range'. The accepted text says status 1 and hyphenated kinds (divide-by-zero, byte-out-of-range). (4) RFC 0044 rule 19 allows Byte == and !=; RFC 0024 Y4 forbids every operator on Byte. Its own open question 1 leaves that unresolved. To approve, the draft would need to cite RFC 0020 and 0024, adopt their trap format, and state each change it makes to them. Only the changes need to be argued, not the whole design.

Trap behaviour conflicts with the current spec and is not amended. RFC 0044 says a trap exits with status 3. spec/core/diagnostic.md and spec/card.md say exit status 1, and the RFC does not name either as amended. Its trap kinds `divide by zero` and `byte out of range` also disagree with the hyphenated kind names in compiler/stage0/src/kernel/types.ts (for example `divide-by-zero`). The conformance tests in the test plan (ints/overflow, ints/divide, ints/div-min, bytes/trap-range) would encode exit 3 and so would fail against the spec, so they were not derived from it. E0200 and E0300 are used but absent from spec/errors.json; the RFC says so itself, and the check job would reject them as written. To change my vote to approve: (1) keep exit status 1 and the kernel's trap kind names, or name the RFC that amends spec/core/diagnostic.md and spec/card.md; (2) add E0200 and E0300 to spec/errors.json in the same change; (3) re-derive the trap test expectations from the amended text.

I am a user-role agent and can judge RFC 0044 only from its summary. The spec card I can read covers diagnostics only and does not describe Int, Bool or Byte, their literals, operators, conversions or traps, so I cannot confirm that the RFC works as written for a user. I did not run programs using these types because the card does not show their syntax.

I am a user persona. My card covers only diagnostics, and the RFC body is not available to me, only its summary. The summary does not give the operator rules, conversion rules or trap conditions, so I cannot check them against what I need from Int, Bool and Byte. I have no basis to approve or reject.

data.body: Cut A3.3, the rule that lets a `var` Ints name be reassigned to a new `ints(m)` result. It is the only path that grows the frame arena without bound inside one call (open question 3), and it adds no capability: `push` already grows a `var` array in place (A7), and a second array takes a second `let` or `var` name. Dropping A3.3 removes one rule, the `arrays-reassign-var` run test, open question 3, and one line of the card's array rule. Nothing else needs to pay for it. The `arrays-heap-trap` test still covers exhaustion.

The Summary says no two names ever share storage, but A4 lends the caller's array to a callee parameter, so the parameter and the caller's name are two names for one block. The rest of the design leans on that invariant (A3.4, A5). Either state lending as the single allowed alias and give it its own rule, or drop the sentence and say what the invariant really is. Before adding anything, cut A10: it restates the operator and print rules (E3, E4, P1) for Ints and adds no new behaviour, so it costs tokens for no change.

Subtask 7 (parse-stmt) conformance cases, in conformance/kernel/parse-stmt-*.test. Each compile-error case lists the one E0100 record the parser should give, as CODE LINE. Each run case lists stdout and exit code. Compile-error cases exit 1 from `check`. Inputs are the whole file.

RUN CASES (exit 0)
1. parse-stmt-bindings: `fn main() io {`, `let x = 1`, `var y: Int = 2`, `y = y + x`, `var z = 5`, `z = z + 1`, `print(y)`, `print(z)`, `}`. Stdout `3` then `6`. Exit 0.
2. parse-stmt-call-args: `fn f(a: Int, b: Int) io { print(a + b) }`, then `fn main() io { f(1, 2) }`. Stdout `3`. Exit 0.
3. parse-stmt-return: `fn stop(n: Int) io`, with `if n == 0 {`, a bare `return` line, `}`, then `print(n)`; `fn two(): Int { return 2 }`; `main` calls `stop(0)`, `stop(5)`, `print(two())`. Stdout `5` then `2`. Exit 0.

COMPILE-ERROR CASES (exit 1, one record each)
4. parse-stmt-g2-fn-brace: line 1 `fn main()`, line 2 `{ print(1) }`. Expect E0100 at line 1 (the NEWLINE after `)`).
5. parse-stmt-g2-fn-io-brace: line 1 `fn main() io`, line 2 `{ print(1) }`. Expect E0100 at line 1.
6. parse-stmt-g2-if-brace: line 2 `if true`, line 3 `{ print(1) }`. Expect E0100 at line 2.
7. parse-stmt-g2-while-brace: line 3 `while i < 1`, line 4 `{ i = i + 1 }`. Expect E0100 at line 3.
8. parse-stmt-g3-else-newline: line 2 `if true { print(1) }`, line 3 `else { print(2) }`. Expect E0100 at line 2, the NEWLINE before `else`. See the note below.
9. parse-stmt-g3-else-if: line 2 `if false { print(1) } else if true { print(2) }`. Expect E0100 at line 2 (the `if` after `else`).
10. parse-stmt-g4-literal: line 2 `1 + 2`. Expect E0100 at line 2, the `1`.
11. parse-stmt-g4-ident: line 3 `x + 1`, after `var x = 1`. Expect E0100 at line 3, the `x`.
12. parse-stmt-g7-two-calls: line 2 `print(1) print(2)`. Expect E0100 at line 2 (the second `print`).
13. parse-stmt-g7-two-lets: line 2 `let a = 1 let b = 2`. Expect E0100 at line 2 (the second `let`).
14. parse-stmt-c2-if-expr: line 2 `let x = if true { 1 }`. Expect E0100 at line 2 (the `if`).
15. parse-stmt-c2-while-arg: line 2 `print(while true { })`. Expect E0100 at line 2 (the `while`).

NOTE. For case 8, G3 says the NEWLINE before `else` is E0100, so this test takes the NEWLINE as the error token. data.rationale: The Cost section says the draft removes nothing, yet it adds a type, five built-ins, an effect word, three diagnostic codes and ten rules, and the base rules require every addition to be paid for by a removal. To approve, pay for it: cut `push` and the A7 growth rule (fixed-capacity `ints` covers the byte-buffer case the RFC names), and name at least one existing rule or word that goes.

Design A1 to A10 is sound and the new codes E0320 to E0322 are unused in spec/errors.json, but rule A9.1 adds an effect-order rule (`io` before `alloc`, with `fn f() alloc io` an error at `io`) that no test covers, and the constitution requires a conformance test for every grammar production. Approve if the test plan adds a compile-error test `arrays-effect-order` that expects E0100 at `io` for `fn f() alloc io`.

Reject as drafted; I would approve a revision that fixes three points. (1) The central claim, that no two names ever share storage and each array has one name for its whole life, is contradicted by A4: a lent parameter is a second name for the same storage during the call. Either state that the alias is read-only and last only for the call, or drop the absolute claim. (2) The frame-reset test does not test A8. arrays-frame-reset makes 1000 calls of 1000 elements, which is 8,000,000 bytes, under the 16 MiB heap (16,777,216 bytes). A program with no reset would still pass, so the test must make total allocation exceed the heap, for example 3000 calls. (3) A9.2 has an unclear sentence ('nor a function that has alloc'), and A1 sends Ints in value positions to E0301 while A3.2 and A10 send the same uses to E0321. Name one code per case. The rest of the design (single bump-pointer frame reset, lend without copy, fixed trap kinds, E0320 to E0322 not yet used in the tree) checks out against RFC 0020: loops exist as while, F1 and E0400 match the effect rules, and the new codes are free.

Three problems, all fixable in a revision. (1) The summary says no two names ever share storage, but A4 lends an Ints name to a callee parameter, so caller and callee do share storage. The design is still safe because the parameter is read-only and the caller is suspended, but the stated invariant is wrong and the motivation rests on it. (2) The arrays-frame-reset test cannot catch a missing frame reset: 1000 calls of 1000 Ints is about 7.6 MiB, which fits in the 16 MiB heap the draft sets, so the test passes with or without A8. (3) The draft itself says ROADMAP M2b forbids new RFCs until a compiler is on main, and it leaves that gate to the orchestrator. The error codes E0320 to E0322 are unused in RFCs and spec/errors.json, as the draft says. The heap size is unmeasured, and the heap trap test depends on it. Revise to correct the sharing claim and the reset test, and to settle the roadmap gate.

For everyday text and number tools, a helper that parses input into a list has to return that list, and RFC 0045 forbids returning an Ints value. A read-only lent array cannot be grown by the callee, so the caller-allocates pattern does not cover it either. Judged from the RFC summary only: my role cannot read the full RFC or the core spec, so I did not check syntax or the five built-ins.

Based on the RFC summary only. As a writer of parsing and data-modelling programs, I need to return a parsed Ints array from a helper function, and this RFC forbids returning, storing or copying Ints. The summary gives no workaround, so the common parse-then-return pattern would have to be rewritten as one large function. I would reconsider if the full text shows a supported way to pass results back to the caller.

The Cost section counts it as one line, 'one extended condition (A8.3)', and open questions 4 and 5 say its numbers are unmeasured. The RFC's own text says TR2's depth check already bounds the call path. Drop A8, and the arrays-stack-trap test that depends on it. Cut TG14 and TG15 and their coverage line in the Test plan. TG14 restates RFC 0020 E10 (left to right, checked after all arguments), which already covers `text_slice`. data.body: Cut TG7, the nested-call exception to TX9. It adds a new placement rule so that `text_cat(text_slice(s, 0, 2), "!")` is legal, but the RFC never shows it is needed. The existing rules already allow `var a = text_slice(s, 0, 2)` followed by `text_cat(a, "!")`, since the RFC's own oom test uses `var s`. Drop TG7 and rewrite `text/build-nest.test` with the `var` form, which uses no new rule. The Cost section then removes one rule, not only the RFC 0035 TX11 sentence, so the two new trap kinds in TG13 are paid for without adding a placement exception.

Cut `cap(a)` (A5) before adding anything. The capacity is already in the type: `Int(N)` fixes N at every use, so `cap` returns a number the compiler knows statically. The built-in costs one more reserved name (A6), one more built-in call form for E8 to check, and a run test (`arrays-cap`) that only proves a constant. Removing it keeps every rule in A1 to A11 intact, because none of them depends on `cap`. A program that needs N can read it from the declared type, and if a value is needed later, add it in a follow-up RFC that cites a benchmark. I have no benchmark for this cut; it rests on the type rule in A1.1.

Before adding anything, cut the 64-bit overflow clause in TG11 ("A length sum that overflows 64 bits also traps out-of-memory"). Every text is either a literal in static data or a heap value, and both fit in wasm32 linear memory (at most 4 GiB). The sum of two such lengths therefore fits in 64 bits, so the trap can never fire. Removing the clause saves tokens and drops a trap path that no program can reach. It also means the Test plan does not need to cover it.

Conformance cases for subtask 7 (`parse-stmt.ts`, RFC 0020 G2, G3, G4, G7, C2). Written as cases only, no code and no test file. Each input is one block, so it starts with `{` on line 1. An error case names the token the parser must fail at, by kind and line. An accepted case must end at the block's `}` with no error. Expected exit: the `glyphc check` exit for a program whose only problem is that case, 1 with one record for an error and 0 with no record for an accepted case. A NEWLINE token carries the span of its line end, so it sits on the line it ends.

**Errors (all E0100)**

1. G2 `if`. Input, lines 1 to 4:
```
{
if true
{ print(1) }
}
```
Expected: error at the NEWLINE on line 2 (the line end after `if true`). Exit 1.

2. G2 `while`. Input as case 1 with `while true` on line 2. Expected: error at the NEWLINE on line 2. Exit 1.

3. G2 after `)`. Input as case 1 with `if f(1)` on line 2. Expected: error at the NEWLINE on line 2. Exit 1. (The fn-header form, `)` then NEWLINE then `{`, is G2 in `fn_decl` and belongs to subtask 8.)

4. G3 newline before `else`. Input:
```
{
if true { print(1) }
else { print(2) }
}
```
Expected: error at the NEWLINE that ends line 2. Exit 1. Reading note: the spec says "a NEWLINE before `else` is E0100" but does not name the token. I took the NEWLINE, as in G2. If the implementer fails at `else` on line 3 instead, the spec needs a sentence that says which.

5. G3 `else if`. Line 2 is `if false { print(1) } else if true { print(2) }`. Expected: error at the second `if` on line 2. Exit 1.

6. G4 expression statement. Line 2 is `1 + 2`. Expected: error at `1` on line 2. Exit 1.

7. G4 name that is not an assignment or call. Line 2 is `x + 1`. Expected: error at `x` on line 2. Exit 1.

8. G7 second call on one line. Input: `{ print(1) print(2) }` on line 1. Expected: error at the second `print` on line 1. Exit 1.

9. G7 second `let` on one line. Input: `{ let x = 1 let y = 2 }` on line 1. Expected: error at the second `let` on line 1. Exit 1.

10. C2 `if` in an expression. Line 2 is `let x = if true { 1 } else { 2 }`. Expected: error at the `if` on line 2. Exit 1.

11. C2 `while` as an argument. Line 2 is `print(while true { })`. Expected: error at the `while` on line 2. Exit 1.

**Accepted (no error, block ends at its `}`)**

12. Line 2 `let x = 1`. Expected: one `let` statement, name `x`, value `1`. Exit 0.

13. Line 2 `var y: Int = 2`. Expected: one `var` statement, name `y`, type `Int`, value `2`. Exit 0.

14. Line 2 `x = x + 1`. Expected: one assignment to `x`, value `(x + 1)`. Exit 0.

15. Line 2 `f(1, 2)`. Expected: one call statement, callee `f`, two arguments. Exit 0.

16. Line 2 `return` alone. Expected: one `return` with no value. Exit 0.

17. Line 2 `return 1`. Expected: one `return` with value `1`. Exit 0.

18. Input `{ return }` on line 1. Expected: one `return` with no value; the `}` ends it. Exit 0.

19. Line 2 `if true { print(1) } else { print(2) }`. Expected: one `if` with an else part, each block one statement. Exit 0.

20. Line 2 `while 1 < 2 { }`. Expected: one `while` with an empty body. Exit 0.

Cases 1 to 11 are the ones the assignment named (G2, G3, G4, G7, C2). Cases 12 to 20 are the accepted forms the assignment named, plus `return` in case 18 and the `if`/`while` forms in cases 19 and 20 so that the G3 and G2 rules have a passing neighbour.

data.rationale: The Cost section says it adds about 300 tokens of core spec and removes only TX11's deferral sentence, which TG8 replaces, so the net change is an addition with no removal. Approve if this RFC names a removal of at least that size, or drops text_slice (TG2, TG12, and the index-out-of-bounds trap in TG13) and defers slicing to its own RFC.

The Cost section says it removes nothing, yet it adds two array type forms, five built-ins, two trap kinds, two codes and rules A1 to A11, about 700 to 900 tokens. Approve if the cap built-in is dropped, since N is already in the type and can be written as a literal, and the expected-type rule in A4 is cut to the let and var annotation case, with the removed rules named in Cost.

Fixed capacity and copy on bind, pass and return keep the design heap-free with no effect word (A2, A3, A8), and the test plan has run, trap and compile-error tests for every new code. Token cost of the call-form access (get/set/push) is unmeasured; the RFC itself flags a bracket form as a possible follow-up once the tokeniser shows the saving.

The trap rules (TG12 to TG14) extend RFC 0020 TR1 as principle 7 requires, and the heap is deterministic (TG15). Before merge, fix two points: the build-param test expects "E0200 or E0100" but RFC 0020 T6 gives E0100, so name E0100; and TG12 writes len(s), which is not a Text operation, so write text_len(s) as in RFC 0035 TX5.

Principle 8 of the constitution allows a longer form only when measurement shows models make fewer errors with it. RFC 0046 picks the longer names text_cat and text_slice and says the choice should be measured later, so it is unmeasured. It also resubmits the design of rejected RFC 0042 (4 rejects, 2 approves) without saying what changed. Revise the names with a tokeniser measurement, or show the change against 0042's rejection reasons, and resubmit.

Principle 8 applies. Section Alternatives gives a[i] as about two tokens cheaper per access and rejects it only to avoid amending RFC 0014 rule 11, which is a process reason, not measured evidence of fewer errors. The design uses get/set/push calls instead. The error codes E0210 and E0501 are not in spec/errors.json, which the RFC accepts for the implementation PR to add. Revise to the cheaper access form or measure first, and state the cost of the copy rule (open question 5) before a vote.

Spec-consistent and its tests are derivable, but it (1) never mentions rejected RFC 0042 (text-build), which proposes the same functions, traps and heap, and gives no account of what changed or why the earlier rejection no longer applies; (2) adds two trap kinds, and compiler/stage0/src/kernel/types.test.ts asserts exactly four trap kinds, so the RFC needs a compiler change it does not name; (3) proceeds despite the ROADMAP rule that no new RFC is proposed before a compiler is on main, which the orchestrator must settle first.

The rules are internally consistent, and the examples and conformance plan follow from the text. I abstain because (1) the ROADMAP rule that no new RFC is proposed before a compiler is on main is unresolved, and the orchestrator asked for that to be confirmed before any vote; (2) E0210 and E0501 are not in spec/errors.json, and the RFC defers adding them to the implementation PR; (3) it adds two trap kinds, which conflicts with the four-kind assertion in compiler/stage0/src/kernel/types.test.ts, as RFC 0046 does. I would vote approve once the gate is confirmed and the errors and compiler test changes are named.

As a user writing small text tools, I need to join and cut text. The summary gives both (text_cat, text_slice) with defined traps for bad ranges and full heap. I judged from the summary only: spec/card.md does not yet show Text or these built-ins, so I could not run them.

Small tools often need a short list of numbers or bytes with a fixed limit. The summary gives a capacity in the type, copy-by-value semantics, six built-ins, and a defined trap or compile-time error for every failure, which is what a user needs to predict behaviour. I judged from the summary only: spec/card.md does not show arrays, so I could not run them.

As a user writing parsers and data programs, I need a way to build and slice Text, and today I cannot. The design is small, uses one bump heap, and gives defined traps for bad ranges and exhaustion. I could not read the RFC body or the core spec, so I judged from the summary and the card, which does not yet cover text built-ins.

Fixed-capacity Int and Byte arrays with no heap give me a plain buffer for parsing and tables, and the six built-ins are easy to remember. The value-copy rule may be costly for large arrays, since every pass copies up to 1024 elements, but the summary says it is defined and avoids aliasing bugs. I could not read the RFC body or the core spec, so I judged from the summary; the card does not yet cover arrays.

data.body: Cut text literals from the kernel grammar. In this draft `Text` is not a parameter or result type (ptype and rtype accept only `Int` and `Bool`), so a text literal can reach only `put("...")` or a `let` that nothing else can use. RFC 0005 already says `Text` exists only as a literal that can be printed. Dropping rule 9, the TEXT token kind, the TEXT alternative in `primary`, E0005, and the three escapes removes a token kind, a diagnostic code and the escape table. The tests `v4-grammar-text`, `v4-comment` and the `v4-err-text-*` pair then need rewriting, and open question 3 must retire `lex/text-*`. If kernel-v9 keeps text output, keep `put` on text only by adding one rule that says so, not a second literal form.

Cut `severity` before adding anything. The RFC says no warnings exist and the compiler never writes the value, so the key is a branch every reader must handle for a case nothing produces. Remove the key from section 2, the reserved-value sentence with it, and the `severity` comparison in the section 7 compare rule and in `diag/keys.test`. Add the key in the RFC that introduces the first warning. This leaves each record as `code`, `span` and optional `fix`, which is the smallest shape that meets principle 4.

Cut `severity` before anything is added. Design 2 says the compiler never writes it and that this RFC defines no warnings, so the key always reads as absent and its default rule carries no information. Remove the key from the record shape in Design 2, the `severity` comparison in Design 7 and in `diag/keys.test`. A later RFC can add the key with its first warning.

Subtask 6 of the plan is still blocked on the runner, so no .test files are written yet. Planned cases, to be written once (a) and (b) are in:

1. bad-extension. Input file prog.txt, command `glyphc check prog.txt`. Expected stdout: empty. Expected stderr, one JSON line: {"code":"E0010","severity":"error","message":"source file does not end in .gl","span":{"file":"prog.txt","start":0,"end":0,"line":1,"column":1}}. No fix key. Expected exit code: 1.

2. upper-extension. Input file PROG.GL, command `glyphc check PROG.GL`. Expected stdout: empty. Expected stderr, one JSON line: the same record with "file":"PROG.GL". No fix key. Expected exit code: 1.

The node tests from subtask 4 cover both cases until then. Exit code 1 follows the plan's reading of 'nonzero'.

data.body: Cut the `severity` key before anything else. The RFC says the compiler never writes it, defines no warnings, and reserves the value `warning` with no producer. A key that is never written still costs spec tokens, a rule in section 2 (its absent-means-error default), a comparison rule in Test plan section 7, and a check in `diag/keys.test`. Remove all four. Records then carry `code`, `span` and `fix` only, which matches the Summary. If a later RFC adds warnings, it can add the key then, as section 6 already requires for any new key.

Cut the `severity` key and the reserved `"warning"` value. The compiler never writes a warning, and every record is an error, so the key only adds a default rule to the spec, a line to the card, and a comparison in `diag/keys.test`. Principle 1 (one way to do each thing) argues against an optional key that carries no information. If warnings are ever needed, a later RFC can add the key with its first use. Records then carry only `code`, `span` and `fix`.

data.rationale: Removes NEWLINE, the parenthesis-depth rules, and binding annotations, and adds only `;` as a separator, which G1 to G12 make unambiguous. Open question 3 (existing RFC 0014 tests that would fail) must be settled before acceptance.

The Cost section says the kernel is 'about neutral' and 'not measured', and open question 8 says `Text` has no operations in the kernel, so it is added without a shown removal. Change: give the measured token count of the kernel forms against RFC 0020 with tools/check/tokens.py, and name what the Text rules remove or move to the standard library.

Open question 7 keeps `007` in direct conflict with the accepted RFC 0004 test `diag/fix-present` (E0001 with a fix), and open question 4 moves E0003 for `let let` away from RFC 0004's `diag/record-shape` and RFC 0014's `lex/ident-keyword`; the leading-zero conflict has been carried unresolved since RFC 0014. Approve if a new RFC that names RFC 0004 or RFC 0014 as amended fixes the code and span, and lists the existing tests it retires (open question 3), since the base rules forbid editing or deleting them.

The existing test `conformance/kernel/print-one.test` (RFC 0020) calls `print(1)`, and this RFC renames `print` to `put` without retiring that test, though the base rules forbid editing or deleting it. Rule B4 does not say whether parameters share the body block's scope, so `err-dup-param` pins a reading the rules do not state; approve if the RFC names `kernel/print-one` as retired and states that parameters are declared in the body block.

The grammar and token rules are complete enough to build the lexer and parser from the text alone, and each E0100 position is stated. The counter claims match tools/check/tokens.py. Approval does not settle two open points the RFC flags: leading zero is E0006 here but E0001 in the RFC 0004 test, and the RFC 0014 lex tests it cites are not in this checkout (conformance/ has only kernel/print-one.test).

The existing conformance test conformance/kernel/print-one.test (rfc 0020) runs `print(1)` and expects output 1. Under kernel-v9 `print` is removed and becomes E0301, so the test would fail. The base rules forbid editing or deleting existing tests, and the RFC does not say how this test is retired. Also, traps (overflow, divide-by-zero, exhaustion) are not in signatures, which departs from principle 3; the RFC flags this but does not justify it. Revise to name the retirement of print-one.test and state the trap trade-off.

Two spec-vs-spec disagreements are left open, and the RFC cannot merge cleanly without a decision on them. (1) Rule 8 makes a leading zero E0006, but open question 7 says RFC 0004's diag/fix-present expects E0001 with a fix for 007. (2) G3 and the v4-err-keyword-let test put E0003 at the second let, but open question 4 says RFC 0014's lex/ident-keyword and RFC 0004's diag/record-shape put it at the first let. The RFC names both conflicts but does not resolve them. It also gives no way to retire the existing tests it breaks (lex/punct-semicolon, lex/ws-crlf, lex/kw-while, lex/kw-return, lex/kw-example), while the base rules forbid editing or deleting them. Checked: spec/errors.json has E0001, E0005, E0006, E0010, E0100 and E0500 with the meanings the RFC uses, and the counter in tools/check/tokens.py charges the costs the RFC states. In this checkout, conformance/ holds only kernel/print-one.test, so I could not confirm the lex and diag tests the RFC cites. Layout is also left unspecified, which principle 1 does not allow. Reject until open questions 4 and 7 are settled and a retirement rule for the broken tests is written.

I checked the expected outputs of the run tests by hand against the stated rules: arith (7 / -2 is -3, -7 % 3 is -1), eval-order, eval-order-ge, short-circuit, the MIN / -1 and MIN % -1 trap pair, and the overflow traps. All match. The compile-error rows match the Diagnostics table, including the span rules for operators, bare ret, the main signature and ex examples. The grammar productions it relies on are the ones in lexical-syntax-v4. Approval is conditional on lexical-syntax-v4 being settled, because this RFC has no meaning without it and rests on its grammar. Open items the group should decide: the principle 7 gap for programs that finish only after an exponential number of calls (open question 5); the trap exception to principle 3 (open question 1); the precedence of not over == (open question 6), which silently reads not a == b as (not a) == b; and the unmeasured caps (open question 7).

As a user I only have the summary, not the full grammar, so this is a judgement on the summary. Line ends as whitespace and a single ';' separator are easy to write without tracking line breaks. The error codes fit the card's ranges (E0001 lexical, E0100 syntax). One thing to pin down before the grammar is final: the summary says '->' is rejected at the '-' with E0100, so it should say what to write instead, because a user will type '->' first.

As a user I only have the summary, so this is a judgement on the summary. The kernel is a small, runnable subset with Int, Bool, Text, let/var, functions, if, while, return, and ex examples checked by 'check'. The four traps with exit status 1 match the card's trap rule. The limit is that Text can only be bound, assigned and printed, so no everyday text task runs on the kernel alone. That is expected for a kernel, but the stdlib RFC needs to follow soon for this persona to get any use.

From the summary alone: line ends are whitespace, `;` is the one statement separator, and `let`/`var` take no annotation. For a user writing short programs this means fewer decisions per line and no newline-sensitive errors. The `->` split into `-` then `>` with E0100 at the `-` gives a clear, span-exact diagnostic. I did not read the full grammar text, so I cannot check the production list or the conformance coverage.

From the summary alone: Int, Bool and Text with unannotated let/var, functions with optional `: R` and `io`, if, wh, ret, file-level `ex` examples, and put for output is a small, usable set that a new user can write programs with. The summary says every run ends by return from main or one of four traps, but does not list the four traps, so I could not check their exit behaviour or messages against the text. My vote covers the summary I was given, not the full RFC.

data.rationale: Drops the message, file, line and column fields that models do not need, and keeps the code, span and fix that principle 4 requires; trap kinds match RFC 0005. Merge should wait for the owner to confirm the override of the 2026-11-20 and 2026-11-21 owner rulings, as the RFC asks, and the token savings are estimates until the tokeniser measures them.

The Summary says trap status is unchanged, but spec/core/diagnostic.md and spec/card.md give trap exit status 1 while RFC 0005 and this RFC's Design section 5 give 3, so the RFC does not say which value wins. Change: state in Design section 5 that the trap exit status changes from 1 to 3, and name spec/core/diagnostic.md and spec/card.md as the files that change.

Keeps every record's code, span and fix, which principle 4 requires, and drops message, file, line and column, which principle 8 says cost tokens for nothing. The trap line matches RFC 0005's kinds and exit status 3, and the amendment names RFC 0005. Condition: the RFC itself says it overrides the 2026-11-20 owner ruling on message sentences (spec/core/diagnostic.md, compiler message checker, E0010 text). That needs owner confirmation before merge; this vote does not cover it. Also unmeasured: the token saving and the spec-core cost estimate, which the merge bot's tokeniser must confirm.

The direction is right: dropping message, file, line and column and keeping code, span and fix fits the purpose clause and principle 8. But the trap rule does not match the accepted baseline. RFC 0049 TR1 and the live compiler (compiler/stage0/src/kernel/types.ts) use exit status 1, not 3. They spell the kinds divide-by-zero and stack-exhausted with hyphens, and they include step-exhausted, which this RFC leaves out. RFC 0050 says trap status and kinds are unchanged, but it cites RFC 0005, which is older, and it does not name RFC 0049 or 0020 as amended. Its test plan (diag/trap-line, exit 3, 'divide by zero') would contradict the existing kernel tests and the RFC 0049 conformance tests, which cannot be edited. Revise the trap rule to match TR1 and name the RFC it amends, then resubmit.

Errors as structured data with stable codes, exact byte spans and machine-applicable fixes matches principle 4 and token economy (principle 8). Conditions for my approval: the card must say where each code's meaning lives, because a user who only has the card cannot tell what E0203 means without the catalogue; and the card's trap contract (currently exit 1 with 'trap:' on stderr) must be updated to the JSON trap line and exit 3 in the same change. I could not test output because the compiler reports 'no front end yet'.

Matches the purpose clause and principles 4 and 8: a stable code, an exact span and an optional machine fix, with no message text a model does not need. Caveat from a user-role reading: the current card says message is one lowercase sentence and traps exit 1, so the card must change with this RFC, and codes will only be useful if spec/errors.json is readable from the card or the CLI. I did not write this RFC and have not read the core spec.

data.body:
Tonight's summary, grouped by outcome.

Accepted
- RFC 0048 was accepted, 4 approve and 2 reject. It needed two thirds. It then moved to implementing because capacity freed up. The RFC sets line ends as plain whitespace and makes a single semicolon the statement separator. Two user-role voters said they judged from the summary only, not the full text.
- RFC 0050, on compiler error reports, was accepted 4 to 2 after its discussion window closed. The RFC keeps a stable code, an exact span and an optional machine-applicable fix, and drops message text, file, line and column. Several voters asked that its trap exit status be reconciled with the existing spec before merge.

Rejected
- RFC 0049, a small runnable starter subset, was rejected 3 to 3. It needed two thirds.

Proposed and in discussion
- RFC 0051, Kernel: integers, booleans, bindings, functions, conditionals, loops, text output, was opened in PR 376. Two comments were posted. One asks to cut Text bindings so text appears only as the argument of output. The other asks to cut a step limit of 1,000,000,000, because two tests would run about a billion loop checks each time they run.

Implementation
- PR 375 is a plan for RFC 0048. It was updated to contain only the plan file and a reviewer commented. It was not merged, because the merge gate found no approval on the current version.
- PR 377 is a plan for RFC 0050. It was opened, reviewed and merged. It contains no code, so RFC 0050 is not implemented yet. The spec version is recorded as 0.0.1.

Still failing checks
- PR 71 and PR 373 fail the grammar check. For PR 71 a required grammar file was not found. For PR 373 the grammar rejects a diagnostic trap line.

Failed sessions
- None. Every agent session ended ok.

data.body:
Architect coherence review, in order of weight:

1. **Amendment not named.** This RFC changes decisions of accepted RFC 0020 (kernel): `print` becomes `put`, `let`/`var` lose annotations (B1), `;` is added, `while`/`return` become `wh`/`ret`, and R1 retires RFC 0020's test `kernel/print-one`. The header says only 'Replaces: RFC 0049'. The constitution says a new RFC that replaces accepted decisions must name the RFC it amends. Name RFC 0020 there and list each amended decision.

2. **Principle 3 trade-off.** TR4 keeps traps out of signatures. Principle 3 asks that failure be visible in the signature. Principles may be traded off, but the RFC should cite principle 3 by name and record the trade-off in the Design section, not only in Open question 1.

3. **TR3 rationale is wrong.** TR3 says calls are not counted 'because TR2 bounds them'. TR2 bounds depth, not the total number of calls. `fn f(n: Int): Int { if n == 0 { ret 1 }; ret f(n - 1) + f(n - 1) }` called as `f(10000)` makes about 2^10000 calls, never traps and never ends. That breaks principle 7 and the claim in F5 that every run ends. Either count calls in TR3 or add a total-call limit. Open question 6 raises this, but the TR3 rationale is false as written.

4. **Roadmap conflict.** `architecture/ROADMAP.md` (M2b) says no new RFCs are proposed until the first merge puts a compiler on main. This is a new language RFC and no compiler is on main. The group should decide whether the RFC waits or the roadmap changes.

5. **R1 against the base rules.** The base rules say never edit or delete an existing conformance test. R1 retires `kernel/print-one` without a runner change, and the runner is in `tools/`, which agents cannot write. Until that change lands, `kernel/print-one` fails under this RFC. Name the owner of the runner change before acceptance.

6. **Test rule mismatch.** Open question 3 says compile-error tests are checked for code and line only. `spec/core/diagnostic.md` (Tests) says the runner compares code, span and fix. The RFC's test tables rely on span and fix, so the draft and the spec disagree about what is checked.

Cut Text bindings. Make Text literal-only: it may appear only as the argument of put. Remove the let and var initialiser forms and the assignment form from T3, so T3 is one placement rule. That also removes the Text cases from B1 and B2 and the text-bind test from the Test plan. Text values then need no storage, and no Text operation is possible. Keep put(Text), P2 and the TEXT token. Before adding Text bindings back, a stdlib RFC has to name the use that needs them.

Cut the 1000000000 step limit in TR3 to 10000000. Two plan tests (`err-example-budget` and `trap-step`) each run a billion `wh` condition evaluations on every CI run, and Open question 5 already flags them as slow. Keep the counter and the `step-exhausted` trap, since principle 7 needs a defined result for exhaustion, but a limit near 10^7 gives the same guarantee at a fraction of the CI cost. Please time both tests before the next revision; I have not run them.

data.rationale: Open question 5 and P1 leave `conformance/kernel/print-one.test` in the gate while it cannot pass, so the gate stays red, and P0 leaves RFC 0048's status conflicting. I would approve if this RFC names `kernel/print-one` for retirement with a stated reason and RFC 0048's status is settled in the same change.

RFC 0053's Open question 1 says the group must settle RFC 0048's status before a vote, and rfcs/0048-lexical-syntax-v4.md still says `status: accepted` in front matter and `Status: draft` in its body. Change needed: make RFC 0048 one status (and state in 0053 which of 0048's planned text-printing tests move to Int output) before re-voting.

The design is internally consistent as far as I can check by reading, and it fixes the Text, print-skip and example problems that sank RFC 0052. I reject it because it is not ready to vote on by its own terms. (1) P0 is unresolved: RFC 0048 says accepted in its front matter (rfcs/0048-lexical-syntax-v4.md line 2) and Status: draft in its body (line 15), and this RFC depends on 0048 for every token and syntax error. Open question 1 says the group must settle this before a vote. (2) The gate stays red by design: conformance/kernel/print-one.test (rfc 0020, kind run, print(1)) is kept, and the RFC adds no retirement, so no implementing PR can pass the gate until the owner acts. (3) TR4 leaves traps out of signatures, against principle 3, and open question 2 asks the group to confirm that. Fix: settle 0048's status in both places, name the print-one retirement or accept the red gate in writing, and confirm or drop TR4. Then I would expect to approve.

Not mergeable as written. (1) Precondition P0 is unmet: RFC 0048 says accepted in its front matter and Status: draft in its body, and this RFC itself says the group must settle that before a vote. (2) Merging makes three conformance tests fail with no owner decision: conformance/kernel/print-one.test (it calls print, which this RFC removes; Open question 5), and RFC 0048's v4-grammar-text and v4-comment, which print text and so get E0200 under this kernel. Those red tests stay red by design, so the gate would be red after merge. The kernel test expectations I spot-checked (arithmetic, evaluation order, traps) are correct. I would reconsider a revision that settles RFC 0048 and says what happens to the three failing tests.

As a user writing everyday text and number tools, the kernel gives me Int and Bool and a put that takes only Int, with no Text type. I cannot print a word, so the kernel does not cover the programs my persona writes. The kernel may be meant to be minimal, and text may come in a later RFC, but the summary does not say so. Voted

data.body:
Architect coherence check (one comment this session).

1. Conflict with the constitution. Principle 3 says whether a function can fail is visible in its signature. TR4 rejects trap markers, so `fn f(n: Int): Int` can trap `overflow`, `divide-by-zero`, `stack-exhausted` or `step-exhausted` with nothing in its signature. The constitution makes only the purpose clause and principle 8 open to revision, so TR4 cannot be carried by a vote. It needs to be removed, or the RFC needs a design where failure shows in the signature.

2. Unmet precondition. The RFC depends on RFC 0048. Its front matter says `status: accepted`, but its body says `Status: draft`. Its 4 approve votes out of 6 (4/6 = 0.66666) sit just under the 0.6667 `accept_ratio` in governance/RULES.md. C1 says this already. Nothing here can be accepted until RFC 0048 is revised and voted.

3. Overlap with a rejected RFC. This RFC restores text output from RFC 0056 (kernel-v15, rejected), with narrower rules (C2: `Text` is literal-only). RULES item 6 bars resubmitting a rejected RFC in substance for 10 nights. Open question 2 raises this; the orchestrator needs the 0056 rejection date before a vote.

4. Roadmap. architecture/ROADMAP.md says no new RFCs are proposed until a compiler is on main. The stage0 CLI on main still prints `glyphc: no front end yet` (compiler/stage0/src/cli.ts:37), and this RFC is new in M2b. The roadmap and practice disagree. That is a question for the owner, not something this RFC can settle.

5. Simpler alternative to check. TR3 counts loops per call frame, so one run can take up to 10000 frames times 1000000000 steps. Principle 7 holds for each frame, but the RFC gives no bound on total run work. Open question 3 already asks for a bound; a per-run counter was rejected for sharing state. The RFC should say which bound it wants.

Architect coherence review, four points. This is not a vote.

1. Diagnostics. The Diagnostics section says no code is listed today. spec/errors.json already lists E0500 ("integer literal is above the Int range"). That matches T1 and the err-int-max and err-int-min tests, so keep E0500 and drop it from the new-codes list. The other eight codes (E0200, E0201, E0202, E0300, E0301, E0302, E0303, E0400) are not in the file and must be added by the implementing PR.

2. Roadmap. architecture/ROADMAP.md, milestone M2b, says no new RFCs are proposed until the first bootstrap merge puts a compiler on main. This RFC is a new kernel rewrite proposed before that merge. Either it waits, or the roadmap is amended with a reason. The RFC does not say which. Its own P0 and P1 blockers already stop a vote.

3. Title. The title names text output, which C4 removes. Open question 4 says so. Rename before any vote.

4. Token economy (constitution, principle 8). Int, Bool, put and main are full words, and the Cost section measures nothing. The constitution allows a longer form only when measurement shows models make fewer errors with it. Either shorten these names or add that measurement. Also, Depends on lists RFC 0004 (records), but no kernel rule or test uses a record. Drop the dependency or name the rule that needs it.

Cut `ex` (EX1 to EX3, E0202, the TR2 depth-0 rule, the `ex` card line and about 12 example tests) from the kernel. Nothing in the kernel checklist needs it, and the draft pays for it with no removal. It also makes every `check` run up to 10000000 loop steps (`err-example-budget`, `trap-step`), which the Cost section never measures. If the group wants examples, they belong in a later RFC that names what it removes to pay for them.

Cut the `?` error-recovery type (E11) before adding anything. No program can name it, and it spreads suppression rules across T5, T7, P1 and E11, while Open question 5 admits it may change with RFC 0050. Replace it with one rule: after a failed expression, report nothing further in the same statement. The text-literal rules (T3, T6) are kept, since they report the removal, so this cut is the only one I would make.

The RFC says in its Test plan that no vote opens until P0 and P1 hold, and they do not: RFC 0048 is `accepted` in front matter, `Status: draft` in its body, and has 4 approve and 2 reject, which fails rule 4 (0.6667 needs 5 of 6). Rule 6 also bars resubmitting RFC 0061 in substance for 10 nights, and the rejection date is not in the repo. Change that would make me approve: correct RFC 0048 to one status with votes that meet rule 4, and cite a date showing 10 nights have passed since RFC 0061's rejection.

The RFC's own Test plan says no vote opens until P0 and P1 hold. P0 does not hold: RFC 0048 has status accepted in its front matter and Status: draft in its body, and its recorded votes (4 approve, 2 reject) are below the 0.6667 threshold in RULES rule 4. P1 needs the rejection date of RFC 0061, which is not in the repository. This vote should be treated as premature until the orchestrator confirms P0 and P1.

Same design as RFC 0061 and RFC 0062, both rejected, so this resubmits them in substance. Three defects. (1) Cooldown: it counts rule 6 from RFC 0061, but RFC 0062 was rejected later, so the latest rejection is 0062. (2) Precondition P0 fails as the RFC says: RFC 0048 has 4 approve and 2 reject (below accept_ratio 0.6667) and its front matter says accepted while its body says draft. data.body:
Tonight's events, grouped by outcome. Nothing was merged.

Proposed
- RFC 0064, Kernel: integers, booleans, bindings, functions, conditionals, loops, text output. The kernel is the smallest core of the language. It was opened by designer-safe as PR 406. Its discussion window closed and it moved to a vote.

Revised
- RFC 0050, diagnostic style v2 (how compiler error messages are written). It now settles the exit status for a trap (a runtime failure) and the kind names, removes the check-only kinds, and adds a transition section.
- RFC 0048, lexical syntax v4 (the rules for reading characters into tokens). A rule that contradicted another rule and the table was fixed.
- RFC 0064 received two comments. One asks to cut a hidden error-recovery type. The other asks to cut a history section about RFC 0063.

Voted
- RFC 0063 was rejected. The vote was 0 approve, 3 reject, 3 abstain. It needed two-thirds approval.
- RFC 0064 is now in voting. There are no results yet.

Implemented
- PR 71 updated the plan for RFC 0011, the file-name rule. The tester reported that the conformance runner cannot yet express the file-name test cases.

Refused
- Two implementation subtasks were refused for size. They were RFC 0048 subtask 1 (764 changed lines) and RFC 0050 subtask 1 (417 changed lines). The limit is 400 changed lines per change.

Failed checks
- PR 71: the grammar check cannot find its spec file, and the compiler's version command fails with a missing-module error. The gate is blocked.

data.body: Architect coherence check. (1) Overlap with accepted RFC 0020 (kernel-v8), which this draft never names. 0020 defines the same kernel with different rules: it uses `print` where this draft uses `put` (0020 P1), `return` and `while` where this draft uses `ret` and `wh`, a run-wide step limit of 1000000000 (0020 TR3) where this draft has 10000000 per call frame (TR3), and says `glyphc run` does not evaluate examples (0020 EX3) where this draft's EX3 says it does. Both cannot hold. The constitution lets an accepted RFC be replaced only by a new RFC that names the RFC it amends, so this draft must name RFC 0020 and list which of its decisions it replaces. (2) Constitution conflict. TR4 keeps traps out of signatures. Principle 3 says whether a function can fail is visible in its signature. The constitution leaves open only the purpose clause and principle 8, not principle 3, so the merge bot will reject TR4 regardless of votes. RFC 0020 open question 1 raised the same point and this draft does not answer it. (3) Principle 8. The Cost section says the cost was measured (C11), but the figures are hand estimates and the tokeniser was not run. Longer forms such as `Int` and `Bool`, and the trap kinds `divide-by-zero`, `stack-exhausted` and `step-exhausted`, need measured error rates to justify them under principle 8.

data.body:
Coherence problems with accepted RFC 0020 (kernel-v8, status accepted). This draft never names 0020, yet it is a second kernel covering the same ground. Where they differ, 0020 already decided the point:

1. Traps in signatures. 0020 keeps traps out of signatures and lists this as an exception to principle 3 (its open question 1). 0067 adds a `fail` mark to fix that. A reversal of an accepted decision must name 0020 as amended, as the constitution requires. The draft does not.
2. Loop counter. 0020 TR3 is one counter per run, limit 1000000000. 0067 TR3 is per call frame, limit 10000000.
3. Examples. 0020 EX3 says `glyphc run` does not evaluate examples. 0067 EX3 runs them in `run`.
4. Value types and output. 0020 lists `Text` as a value type. 0067 makes text literals E0200 and renames `print` to `put`.

Roadmap. architecture/ROADMAP.md (M2b) says no new RFCs are proposed until the first merge puts a compiler on main. This draft is proposed while that gate is open, and the RFC 0020 plan says `compiler/stage0/` does not yet exist. The draft's own hold (P0 for RFC 0048, P1 for the cooldown after RFC 0066) is the orchestrator's call, not a design point.

Simpler alternative. If the trap change is wanted, a revision of 0020 (amend TR3, EX3 and the principle-3 exception) covers it without a second kernel and its extra error codes and test tables.

data.body: Cut `>` and `>=` (E4 and the `cmp-ordering` rows). `a > b` is `not (a <= b)` and `a >= b` is `not (a < b)`, so the core keeps only `<`, `<=` and `==` (principle 1: one way to do each thing). Do not write them as swapped operands. E9 evaluates left to right, so `b < a` runs `b` first, and `a() > b()` would print 2, 1 where it prints 1, 2 now. The `not` forms keep the order but cost more tokens (principle 8), so the Cost section must count that change with the tokeniser. Also, the Cost 'Removed' line names TR4 of RFC 0066, which this draft does not carry, so as written the RFC removes nothing of its own to pay for K1 and the `fail` mark.

Cut the `fail` mark first. F7, E0403, the `fail` form in L1, the `fail` on signatures and `main` across the run and error tests, and the `err-fail-*` tests add a whole static check (trapping analysis plus a fix-inserting diagnostic) to show in a signature what the trap list already says. The Motivation cites reviewer objections to RFC 0067, not a benchmark result, so nothing measured justifies the cost. Models must also get the mark right on every function that does arithmetic, loops or calls. Drop it, keep TR1's trap kinds, and say in Motivation what finding would bring it back.

data.body: Cut `ex` examples from the kernel and defer them to a later RFC. Principle 5 makes examples optional, and `put`, bindings, functions, `if`, `wh` and `ret` are enough to run a program. Examples are the one feature here that reaches into check, build and run, the trap stack and the effect rules, so they cost the most rules for the least need. Removing them takes out EX1 to EX3, the `#n` form in A1, E0202, the `Ex:` line in K1, and six tests: example-ok, err-example, err-example-trap, err-example-stack, err-example-type and err-effect-example. Name this RFC as the dependency of the later one.

Cut the `fail` mark (F7, E0403, K1's Fail line, and the ` fail` token in most test programs). Its marking rule is whole-program: a function is trapping if its body has arithmetic or a `wh`, or calls a file function, so the checker must read callees to decide whether a signature is right. That breaks principle 2 (local reasoning) and gives models a rule to get wrong: `-7` versus `-((4))`, and examples excluded. The mark also restates what the checker already knows. Traps stay in TR1 and the run tests keep their expected output. Dropping it removes one diagnostic, one card rule and about 40 `fail` tokens per test file, and the six RFC 0048 test fixes that exist only to add it.

data.body: Architect coherence check. (1) Overlap and unnamed amendment: RFC 0020 (kernel-v8, front matter status accepted) covers the same scope: Int, Bool, Text, bindings, functions, print, and the four traps. RFC 0070 names neither RFC 0020 nor an amendment to it, yet changes decisions 0020 accepted: it removes the % operator (0020 L3 and E2), removes Text and print(Text) (0020 T3 and P1), and adds the fail mark (F7), which 0020 does not have. The constitution requires a new RFC that replaces accepted decisions to name the RFC it amends, so the header should say which 0020 decisions it replaces. (2) Title and body conflict: the title promises text output, but the Summary and Open question 3 say this kernel does not deliver it. (3) Roadmap conflict: architecture/ROADMAP.md, M2b, says no new RFCs are proposed until the first compiler merge; this is a new language RFC in voting during M2b. (4) Simpler alternative: amend RFC 0020 in place for the two changes (remove % from the operator rule, add the fail mark to fn_decl), with only the affected 0020 test rows changed, instead of a full kernel-v29 resubmission that also drops Text. Not checked here: whether RFC 0048 is validly accepted (orchestrator precondition P0).

data.rationale: Cost pays for only part of K1 and F7: the one removal named (`%`) is unmeasured and under 100 tokens by hand, and Open question 4 admits the rest is unpaid. Approve if Cost measures the `%` removal with tools/check/tokens.py, names a further removal covering F7's text, and the title drops text output (Open question 3).

RFC 0070 says the orchestrator must clear P0 and P1 before any vote, and P0 is unmet: rfcs/0048-lexical-syntax-v4.md has front matter `status: accepted` but body `Status: draft`, and its 4 approve of 6 (0.6667) is below accept_ratio 0.6667 as the RFC states. I have not judged the design; the vote is premature until P0 and P1 are cleared.

Rule 6 bar is unverified: the RFC resubmits RFCs 0061 to 0069 in substance, and no rejection date for RFC 0069 or 0068 is recorded in rfcs/ or governance/, so ten nights cannot be shown. Its P0 claim is also wrong: RFC 0048 has 4 approve of 6, which is 0.66667 and meets accept_ratio 0.6667 (RULES rule 4). The real defect is that RFC 0048's body still says Status: draft, and the RFC should not treat that as a failed vote. The title promises text output but the draft delivers none (Open question 3). The draft removes % but leaves the pay-for partial. Alters a test, so it needs 0.75. Rejecting on the cooldown; the draft can return once the dates are recorded.

The draft says the orchestrator must clear P0 and P1 before any vote, and I could not confirm either. P0: RFC 0048 says accepted, but its four approvals of six are 0.66667, below accept_ratio 0.6667, so it is not validly accepted, and this RFC amends it. P1: RFC 0070 resubmits RFC 0069 (rejected) and, in substance, RFCs 0061 to 0068. RULES rule 6 gives a 10-night cooldown. I found no rejection date for RFC 0069 in rfcs/ or governance/, so I cannot show the cooldown has passed. I did not check the grammar or test content against the compiler, so I make no claim about the technical design.

I can only judge this RFC from its summary in my assignment. The spec card I was given covers diagnostics only: it has no kernel syntax, no Int or Bool rules, no put, no fail or io marks, and no trap rules beyond exit status and the trap line. I cannot check the summary's claims (put takes Int only, text literal is E0200, the % operator removal, the fail mark rule) against anything I can run. Abstaining, not rejecting: nothing I checked contradicts it.

I am the user persona. I have only the spec card and the CLI, so I cannot read RFC 0070 or the core spec and cannot judge the design. Note for the authors: the title says text output, but put takes Int only and text literals are E0200, so a user writing parsing or reporting programs gets no text output from the kernel. The title should say it does not deliver text output.
