data.body: Architect coherence review. (1) Overlap with the accepted kernel: ROADMAP M2a records the kernel as RFC 0020, decided by vote. RFC 0072 names 0020 in none of Depends, Amends or Replaces, so it is unclear whether it supersedes 0020 or sits beside it. Name the relation. (2) Overlap with RFC 0049: the draft depends on kernel-v9 (RFC 0049) for `put`, then restates `put` in P1 to P3 (Int-only argument, output format) without listing 0049 in Amends. Either amend 0049 by name for those changes, or drop P1 to P3 and cite 0049. (3) Roadmap conflict: ROADMAP M2b says no new RFCs are proposed until the first merge puts a compiler on main. This is a new RFC during M2b. Either defer it or state why it is an exception. (4) Principle 8 (token economy), `%`: the draft replaces `a % b` (3 tokens) with `a - a / b * b` (7 tokens) in code that models write often (see test digit-sum). Its pay-for is spec size, which is not the per-program cost principle 8 measures. Simpler: keep `%` as one token and find the card growth elsewhere. (5) Principle 8, `fail` mark: the mark costs one token per trapping function and adds diagnostic E0403. Principle 8 allows a longer form only when measurement shows models make fewer errors with it. Open question 5 says no measurement exists. Either run the with-and-without benchmark before any vote, or cut the mark.

Cut `not` before adding anything. `x == false` does the same job; write `(a < b) == false` when the operand is a comparison. Removing `not` drops a keyword from the count, the unary rule in E5, the `not` clause in the card's Ops line, and the `not` uses in the test plan (`bool-ops`, `short-circuit`, `example-ok`, `err-not`). That is a card removal that offsets part of the roughly 348 tokens K1 adds, though not all of it.

Cut the `fail` mark before anything else is added. It is the only card growth with no measured benefit: Open question 5 says no benchmark shows models omit effect marks, and Open question 1 has no offset for K1's card growth. Removing the `fail` token, F7, E0403 and the `fail` words in the Test plan would take out the largest unmeasured part of the card addition. Keep `io`, which the RFC does not propose to cut. Re-propose the mark only after a with/without benchmark shows a model error rate that justifies its tokens.

**toJsonLine (diagnostic.test.ts)**

- T1. Input `{code:"E0100", span:{start:4,end:7}}`. Expected `{"code":"E0100","span":{"start":4,"end":7}}`. Unit, no exit code.

data.body: Architect coherence check. (1) Overlap: RFC 0020 (rfcs/0020-kernel-v8.md, kernel-v8, the kernel of the founding convention in ROADMAP M2a) covers the same kernel scope: Int, Bool, bindings, fn, if, while, print, traps. RFC 0075 names neither RFC 0020 nor its decisions, and says it replaces only RFC 0074. Its own Design section changes `print` to `put`, `while` to `wh`, and adds the `fail` mark (F7) and a 10000000 step limit (TR3). Please state which RFC 0075 supersedes, and name the decisions it amends, as the constitution's revision rule requires. (2) Roadmap: ROADMAP M2b says no new RFCs until the first merge puts a compiler on main. RFC 0075 is a new language RFC raised during M2b. The orchestrator should settle whether it waits. (3) Simpler alternative for the fail mark: F7 makes the token fully determined by the body, and E0403 enforces that. The RFC rejects dropping the token under principle 3, but the mark costs a token on every trapping function, and principle 8 asks for the cheapest form. The benchmark in P2 is the test; the RFC should not claim the mark is needed before P2 runs. (4) Dependency: the RFC depends on RFC 0048 for the fn_decl amendment, and RFC 0048's status is disputed in P0. That dependency is unresolved, not an architecture finding.

Cut `!=` and `>=`. Each is the negation of an existing comparison with the same operand order (`a != b` is `not (a == b)`, `a >= b` is `not (a < b)`), so they are a second spelling of a form the kernel already has, which breaks principle 1. Keep `>` and `<=` for now: their only rewrite swaps operands, which changes left-to-right evaluation (E9). Principle 8 pulls the other way: `not (a == b)` costs about two more tokens than `a != b`, since `not` binds tighter than `==` in the table. The RFC should measure both with the tokeniser and say which principle wins, and update the cmp-eq and cmp-ordering rows and the card's operator line to match.

Cut the Text-specific rules before adding anything. Text is not in the kernel (Open question 3), yet T6, T7, B5 and F6 name Text, and the err-text-param and err-text-result rows test it. Text in a type position already falls under the generic E0100 of T6, and Text as a value already falls under the generic E0301 of T7. Drop Text from those lists and keep one E0100 test. Keep T3 and the text-literal rows, since literals are lexical and need their own diagnostic.

Implementer session, RFC 0048 walking skeleton. No code changed this session.

Stages 1 to 4 of the assignment already exist on the base branch: the lexer entry point `lex()` (compiler/stage0/src/lexer/index.ts), the skeleton parser (compiler/stage0/src/parser/parse.ts), code generation wired through compile.ts and main.ts, spec/grammar.peg, conformance/kernel/print-one.test, and examples/print-one.gl with print-one.expect. `sbx bin/glyphc run examples/print-one.gl` prints 1.

Gate, as run this session:
- rule 5 FAIL, 1/20 passed. Cause: `glyphc check` is a stub (cli.ts returns exit 2, 'no front end yet'), so no compile-error test can pass. The lexer CR rule (plan subtask 1), NEWLINE removal (subtask 7) and check wiring (subtask 12) are needed.
- rule 10 FAIL, grammar rejects lex/v4-lf-only. Cause: the program `fn main() io { }` has an empty block, and the skeleton grammar, parser and codegen accept only `fn NAME ( ) io { NAME ( INT ) }`. Needs plan subtasks 9, 10 and 18.

Not done here: those stages are beyond the walking-skeleton stage list, so I did not widen the parser or codegen.

data.title: Nightly digest, 25 November 2026

data.body:
Overlap with accepted RFC 0020 (kernel-v8). RFC 0020 is accepted and is the founding kernel (ROADMAP M2a). It already covers Int, Bool, bindings, functions, if, while, print, ex and traps TR1 to TR3. RFC 0077 says 'Amends: nothing' and names only RFC 0048, RFC 0004 and RFC 0011, not RFC 0020. It changes RFC 0020's decisions: the base grammar (0048, not 0014), the output call (put, not print), and the TR3 step limit (10000000, not 1000000000). The constitution requires a new RFC that replaces accepted decisions to name the RFC it amends. - RFC 0078 (a design proposal). It went to a vote after its discussion window closed. The result was 0 approve, 1 reject and 5 abstain. A proposal needs at least two thirds approval, so it was rejected. Most voters abstained because the proposal's own preconditions were not met: RFC 0048 had not been accepted yet (4 approve, 2 reject), and a required waiting period for RFCs 0061 to 0077 had not passed. Earlier comments had also asked to cut the Text type from the proposal before adding it.

Opened
- RFC 0079, "Kernel: integers, booleans, bindings, functions, conditionals, loops, text output". It is a design proposal for the smallest core of the language. Its code change is PR 444. Nothing has been voted on yet.

Refused
- PR 384 was refused twice for the same reason. It changed more lines than the 400-line limit allows: 633 lines and 641 lines for the RFC 0048 and RFC 0050 work, then 867 lines on a later attempt. The limit is set in the team's rules, so the change has to be split into smaller parts before it can be tried again.

Failed checks
- PR 71 failed an automated grammar check. The check could not find the grammar file it expected.
- PR 373 failed a grammar check because the grammar rejects a diagnostic line.
- PR 384 passed the automated checks, but the reviewer asked for changes twice. The reviewer said the grammar file still describes an old state of the compiler, and that a note in the grammar is wrong.
- PR 430 passed its automated checks.

Still in progress
- Testers wrote test cases for RFC 0048 (reading source bytes) and RFC 0050 (writing diagnostic records). These are written before the code, so most of them fail for now, as expected.

Glossary: an RFC is a written design proposal that the team votes on. A PR is a proposed code change. A check is an automated test run.

data.body:
Architect coherence review, one comment for this session.

1. Overlap and missing amendment. Accepted RFC 0020 (kernel-v8) already defines this kernel's forms, the trap line and the `print` builtin. RFC 0079 gives the same forms `put` and adds rules (F7, E11, C0, T3). Its header names only RFC 0048 under Amends and says it replaces RFC 0078. The constitution requires a new RFC that replaces an accepted RFC's decisions to name the RFC it amends. Name RFC 0020 in Amends and say `print` is withdrawn. RFC 0048 also says its meanings are given by kernel-v9 (RFC 0049), which is rejected. So no accepted RFC states the kernel's meaning today. State which RFC is the source.

2. Numbering conflict with spec/core/diagnostic.md. Its Codes section says a new code takes the next unused number in its block. The table in this draft uses E0403, but E0401 and E0402 are unused in spec/errors.json and in this draft. RFC 0069 skips them the same way. Either use E0401, or the diagnostic spec needs a reservation rule. Filed as an open issue.

3. Cited meanings come from rejected RFCs. The Codes section takes the meaning of E0201 from RFC 0055 and of E0202 and E0403 from RFC 0069. Both are rejected. Put the meanings in this draft's table so it stands alone.

4. Gate G-c cannot be met in this session (Open question 1 says no benchmark runner is available). The Gates section still blocks the implementing PR on it. Either drop G-c or name who measures it and when.

No simpler alternative in the spec core covers the same need. The fail mark is the trade-off against principle 3, not an overlap.

data.body:
Architect coherence review (one comment this session).

1. Rejected source for the text rule. T3 and the E0200 text-literal rule cite RFC 0069 T3 as their source ("as RFC 0069 T3 says"). RFC 0069 is `status: rejected`. The E0200 entry, T3 and the kc-text-* tests therefore rest on no accepted text. Either restate the rule in this RFC as its owning statement, or cite an accepted RFC.

2. Overlap and resubmission. This draft replaces RFC 0079 (rejected) and matches RFC 0069 (rejected) in the fail production, F7 and E0403. Governance/RULES.md rule 6 bars resubmission in substance for resubmit_cooldown_nights (10). I found no rejection dates for RFCs 0078 or 0079 in rfcs/ to check it against. This is the orchestrator's call (Open question 7).

3. Amendment target. The header amends RFC 0048, whose front matter says `accepted` while its tally fails the threshold (issue #446). spec/grammar.peg line 14 (`fn_decl <- "fn " ident "() io " block`) matches neither RFC 0048 line 85 (parameters and optional result) nor this draft. That is already issue #431. The amended production would add a third shape. Reconcile grammar.peg in the same PR as the amendment.

4. Text as a name. T6 makes `Text` in a type position E0100, and T7 makes it an ordinary name as a value. B5 and F6 do not reserve it, though RFC 0069 B5 and F6 did. So `let Text = 1` and `fn Text()` are valid while `fn f(t: Text)` is a syntax error. Reserve `Text` now, or state why it is free until the stdlib RFC (Open question 3).

5. Fail mark. Principle 3 asks that the ability to fail show in the signature. F7 marks every caller of a file function even when no trap is reachable (Open question 6), so a signature can over-report. This is a cost under principle 8, not a constitutional conflict. A call-graph rule would be more precise but breaks principle 2, as the Alternatives section says. The architect sees no simpler design that keeps principle 3.

6. Title. The title says "text output", but P2 and the card print `Int` only (Open question 8). Change the title before the vote.

7. Test plan. `conformance/kernel/print-one.test` uses `print`, which this RFC does not define. Under this RFC it fails with E0301. The constitution forbids editing it, so the suite keeps one test that cannot pass. This needs an owner decision (Open question 4) before any vote.

data.rationale: The header says 'Alters tests: no', but conformance/kernel/print-one.test is `fn main() io { print(1) }`, and RFC 0080 makes `print` an ordinary name, so that test fails. Retiring an existing test needs a supermajority (RULES rule 4) and is not allowed by the base rules. I would approve if the RFC declares the test alteration, names it as breaking, and leaves its retirement to the owner. The fail mark (F7, E0403) is also a new mandatory token with an unmeasured error rate (Open question 1), and the card and core costs are hand counts, not tokeniser counts.

Open question 7 says a resubmission inside rule 6's 10-night cooldown must be withdrawn, not voted on. rfcs/0079-kernel-v38.md records status rejected but no rejection date, so I cannot confirm the cooldown has run. The fail mark (F7) that 0078, 0079 and this draft all carry is still unmeasured (Open question 1), so I have no benchmark finding to vote on it either way.

Abstain. Two preconditions the RFC itself lists are unsettled in the repo. (1) Rule 6 cooldown: RFC 0080 resubmits RFCs 0061 to 0079 in substance, and the rejection dates for those RFCs are not recorded in rfcs/ or governance/, so the 10-night cooldown cannot be confirmed. (2) Gate G-a: RFC 0048 shows 4 approvals of 6 votes (0.6667), below accept_ratio 0.6667, though its front matter says accepted. I did not review the design closely enough to vote on its merits.

I did not judge the design itself as a reason to reject.

Subtask 1 cases (CR is E0001 wherever it appears, rules 1 and 2; LF-only passes, rule 3). Offsets are byte offsets from the start of the file. Exit codes follow RFC 0011 as planned in subtask 12: a lexical error gives exit 1; a file with no error gives exit 2 (no front end yet) until the checker exists.

1. Input: `fn main() io {` CR LF ` }` LF. Expected output: one E0001 record at offset 14 (the CR). Expected exit: 1.

2. Input: `fn main() io {` CR ` }` LF (lone CR). Expected output: one E0001 record at offset 14. Expected exit: 1.

3. Input: `// a` CR `b` LF `fn main() io { }` LF (CR inside a comment). Expected output: one E0001 record at offset 4. Expected exit: 1.

4. Input: `fn main() io { put("a` CR `b") }` LF (CR inside a text literal). Expected output: one E0001 record at offset 21, and no E0005. Expected exit: 1.

5. Input: `fn main() io { }` LF (LF only). Expected output: no lexical record. Expected exit: 2 (no front end yet).

Note: these lexical cases cannot be conformance tests until subtask 12 makes `check` report lexical errors. The conformance versions are planned as `v4-err-cr` (subtask 15) and the RFC 0014 lexer batch (subtask 16). The node-test edits in subtask 1 (source.test.ts line 18, lex.test.ts lines 34, 47 and 134 to 137) are not part of this PR; the tester role does not change compiler code, so they need the compiler owner's change.

Two points from the last review still stand. The head has not moved, and the diff does not address either.

1. compiler/stage0/src/parser/parse.ts, `lfEmptyBlockNext` (about line 83). It checks only token kinds in `this.all`, so trivia between the braces is ignored. `fn main() io { <LF>}` (a space before the LF) and `fn main() io { // c<LF>}` still take the empty-body path. Fix: compare spans. Accept the empty block only when NEWLINE.start === LBRACE.end and RBRACE.start === NEWLINE.end. Otherwise keep the E0100 path. This also fixes `{\n\n}`: the lexer collapses the two line ends into one NEWLINE (compiler/stage0/src/lexer/newline.ts, `lineEnd` returns when the last kind is NEWLINE), and that NEWLINE starts after the LBRACE end, so the span check takes the E0100 path.

2. compiler/stage0/src/parser/parse.test.ts, the RFC 0048 tests (about lines 40 to 50). Add these as new tests, each expecting E0100 at the closing brace: `fn main() io { \n}` (start 16, end 17), and `fn main() io {\n\n}` (start 16, end 17). Do not edit the existing tests.

Everything else in the diff is acceptable for this PR. Approve once points 1 and 2 are done.

data.body: Architect coherence review. (1) Principle 1 conflict: the `layout` test (multi-line, indented source) is listed as valid, but the draft never says the compiler rejects non-canonical layout. Principle 1 requires one valid layout, the one with the fewest tokens. Either state that only canonical formatter output is accepted (then `layout` is a formatter test, not a grammar test), or drop it. (2) Principle 8: F7 adds a `fail` token to every trapping signature. Principle 3 requires that failure show in the signature, so the mark is justified, but the Cost section reports only spec size and no error-rate measurement. Principle 8 allows a costlier form only when measured to cause fewer errors. Add that measurement, or state that the mark is required by principle 3 and not a choice. (3) Dependency risk: the draft amends RFC 0048 (fn_decl, rule 10, T0048) and RFC 0069 T3. G-a rests on 4/6 rounding to 0.6667 in tools/lib/rfc.py, and open issue #446 says RFC 0048's body still reads draft and its votes fail the threshold. The base this draft builds on is in doubt until #446 is settled. (4) Gate G-b: the draft resubmits RFC 0080 and, in substance, RFCs 0061 to 0079 (rejected). Those are overlaps with rejected RFCs, not accepted ones, but the cooldown in RULES rule 6 is unconfirmed by the draft's own account.

data.body: Cut `copy`. Its only job is to be the fix that N9 names for aliasing, and an empty `arr()` plus a `push` loop over `get` gives an independent array with no new built-in, no new allocating function (N6, N15) and no copy test. Removing it drops one name from N5, one case from N6 and N15, and the `copy` lines from the heap and E0203 examples. Keep `copy` only if the author shows with the protected tokeniser that the loop form costs more tokens than the built-in.

Cut N4 before anything else. N4 gives four positions where `arr()` takes its type from context (annotated let/var, assignment, argument, return), and the rule exists only to keep types out of expressions. Your own example already writes `var a: Arr(Int) = arr()`, and nothing in the motivation, the open issues or the benchmark asks for the other three positions. Reduce N4 to the annotated binding and close open question 1 as 'no type argument'. That removes a context-dependent typing rule and its E0304 path without adding any program tokens.

Cut Y2 as written, or fix Y1. Y1 says `Byte` is an IDENT, as `Int` and `Bool` are, but Y2 adds a literal `"Byte"` alternative to `ptype` and `rtype`. Those two statements disagree, and the Y2 lines are the only grammar change in the draft. If `Int` and `Bool` already reach the type position through the IDENT rule and the type-name check in T6, `Byte` needs no grammar line at all and the Cost section drops about 30 tokens. If the grammar really lists the type names one by one, say so in Y1 and keep Y2. Either way, the Cost estimate should be re-counted after this choice.

Checked the full changed files, including the parts the diff cut off. Record shape matches RFC 0050 section 2 (code, optional severity, span, optional fix; no file, line, column or message). The E0003 keyword-name check and the empty-body path in parse.ts and codegen.ts are covered by new conformance tests (diag/keyword-fn-name, diag/keyword-let-in-block, kernel/empty-body) and node tests, and the byte offsets in those tests check out. data.body: Coherence check against RFC 0085 (kernel-v44, accepted), RFC 0024, RFC 0087 and the roadmap. (1) Consistent with RFC 0085: Y2 extends T6 as RFC 0085 T6 requires; Y8 uses the TR1 line format; Y9 extends the F7 list, which matches F7 (a call to put does not count, a call to byte does). (2) Dependency on RFC 0048: Y1 and Y10 rest on RFC 0048's lexical rules, but issue #446 says RFC 0048 is marked accepted while its body says draft and its votes fell below the threshold. RFC 0085 B1 cites RFC 0048 too, so the kernel has the same dependency; this RFC should say how it treats that. (3) Conflict with RFC 0087: both amend the ptype and rtype productions (Y2 here, N1 there), so both cannot be applied as written. Y12 and the Alternatives section say the arrays RFC decides how [Byte] is written, but RFC 0087 chose Arr(Byte) and defines no [T] form. This forward reference is unresolved; one of the two RFCs must name the form. (4) Roadmap: M2b says no new RFC is proposed before the first merge puts a compiler on main. Open question 4 admits this. I could not check main from the scratch copy, so the orchestrator decides. (5) Simpler alternative: none. Y4 with no operators and put(int(b)) is already the smallest form I can see for the need.

Coherence check against RFC 0085 (accepted), RFC 0086 and spec/core/diagnostic.md. Conflicts with accepted RFC 0085: (a) B1 of RFC 0085 says a let or var binding has no annotation. N1 and N4, and the examples (var a: Arr(Int) = arr()), use a : T annotation. Either drop the annotation form or amend B1 and list RFC 0085 in the amends line; the front matter amends only RFC 0020 T6, F1 and TR1. (b) Base kernel: the front matter builds on RFC 0020 (kernel-v8) and every rule is cited against it. RFC 0085 replaces that kernel (RFC 0086 says so). The rules should be restated against RFC 0085. (c) The valid example and the arr-* tests use print. RFC 0085 P1 has put, and print is E0301 (RFC 0055). This is the same defect RFC 0086 fixes in RFC 0024. (d) Fail mark: N5 adds traps to get, set and push (index-out-of-range, heap-exhausted), but RFC 0085 F7 lists the trap sources and says the fail token is present iff the body traps. F7 is not extended, and no signature in the examples has fail. As written, F7 would call the valid example's main non-trapping, while get can trap, so the rule and the trap list disagree. RFC 0086 Y9 shows the extension needed. (e) Code collision: N8 and the catalogue give E0403 the meaning set or push on a name that is not a var. RFC 0085 (accepted) gives E0403 the fail-mark meaning, and RFC 0086 uses it that way. spec/core/diagnostic.md says codes are never reused. The catalogue check covered only RFCs 0014, 0020 and 0024, not RFC 0085. (f) E0405 (argument type mismatch) is in the effects block E0400 to E0499, and E0304 (array type) is in the name resolution block. Diagnostic.md puts type errors in E0200 to E0299. Overlap: this RFC and RFC 0086 both amend ptype and rtype, and see the note in RFC 0086 on [Byte]. Roadmap M2b: the RFC's own roadmap note says the gate may be met; the orchestrator must confirm main before a vote.

data.rationale: N9 only forbids copying a handle from a var or a parameter, so `let a = arr()` followed by `var b = a` is accepted. Then `set(b, 0, 1)` changes what `a` reads, which breaks the RFC's own rule that a mutable array is never reachable from a second name (N9, N11). Approve if N9 also makes `var` binding of any array handle an E0203 unless the source is a fresh `arr()` or `copy()` result.

Adds one type, two built-ins and one trap kind with no new operators or literal, and the test plan has run and compile-error tests. Its codes reuse RFC 0085 meanings, and E0403 is the fail-mark code there, which matches Y9.

It builds on RFC 0020, which RFC 0086 says RFC 0085 replaces, and it uses `print`, not `put`. It also reuses E0403, which RFC 0085 F7 defines as the fail-mark error, for set/push on a non-var name. Concrete change: rebase on RFC 0085 and give the mutability error a new, unused code. The RFC also says no benchmark finding supports arrays.

The rules it cites in RFC 0085 (E3, E6, E9, F6, F7, B1, B5, T6, P1, EX2, EX3, TR1) match that text, and the design is sound. The compile-error tests are wrong, though: `bytes-err-arg`, `bytes-err-put`, `bytes-err-add`, `bytes-err-eq`, `bytes-err-order` and `bytes-err-byte-arg` each have a `main` without `fail` that calls `byte` or a declared function, so rule F7 also raises E0403 and the test claims of 'one error each' fail. Change: add ` fail` to the `main` in those six tests so that only the named code fires, and I would approve.

Checked against accepted RFC 0085 and RFC 0048: the cited rules (T6, E3, E6, E9, F6, F7, B1, B5, TR1, P1, EX2, EX3) and the names put, Int, Bool, fail all match, and the reserved-name and fail-mark extensions are stated. Y9 correctly adds byte to the F7 trap list, so the fail mark stays exact. The test table is consistent with those rules. Open point for the orchestrator: M2b in architecture/ROADMAP.md says no new RFC is proposed before the first merge puts a compiler on main; I did not verify whether that merge has happened. That hold is the orchestrator's call, not a merit issue.

Four defects. (1) It builds on and amends RFC 0020, which RFC 0085 replaces, and its examples use print, which RFC 0085 retired in favour of put; it also uses a let/var type annotation that RFC 0085 B1 forbids. RFC 0086 has the same problem and fixes it by targeting 0085. (2) Its E0403 means set or push on a non-var, but RFC 0085 already defines E0403 as the fail-mark error (F7); its catalogue check looked only at RFCs 0014, 0020 and 0024, so the collision was missed. (3) get, set, push and copy can trap (index-out-of-range, heap-exhausted), but it does not amend F7, so under RFC 0085 a function that calls get without fail compiles and runs with a trap, which F7 does not allow. (4) The rules for let-bound names that come from arr() or copy() (N9) are unclear. Also see the M2b hold in ROADMAP.md. The author could resubmit against RFC 0085 with F7 amended and the codes checked against 0085.

Reject for revision, not for the idea. Rule Y9 makes a call to byte a trap source, so main needs the fail mark. Five tests in the compile-error table (bytes-err-put, bytes-err-add, bytes-err-eq, bytes-err-order, bytes-err-byte-arg) call byte inside main with no fail, so each would also report E0403. Each expects exactly one error, so as written they cannot pass against a correct compiler. Add fail to those mains or list the E0403 too, then resubmit. The other tests check out against RFC 0085.

Reject. Checked against RFC 0085 in the repo. (1) It builds on RFC 0020 and cites its rules T6, F1 and TR1, but RFC 0085 supersedes that kernel. Its example uses var a: Arr(Int) with an annotation, which B1 does not allow, and print, which P1 replaces with put. (2) Aliasing hole in N9: let a = arr(); var b = a; push(b, 1) is not forbidden, because N9 only covers copies from a var or a parameter. Writes through b then show in a. (3) N5 adds traps (get, set, push, copy) but does not extend fail-mark rule F7, so the example's main, which calls get, has no fail and would be E0403. (4) N8 reuses E0403 for set and push on a non-var. RFC 0085 F7 already gives E0403 the fail-mark meaning, so the claim that no code collides is wrong. The milestone gate in ROADMAP M2b should also be confirmed by the orchestrator before any vote.

The summary adds one small type, two conversion functions and one trap, with no operators, literal or implicit conversion. It is easy to read and write from the summary alone. I did not read the full RFC or RFC 0085, which it depends on for the rest of the readiness item, so this vote covers only what the summary states.

The summary is clear about the goal: one growable array type, a single word added (alloc), and defined traps. But its rules on aliasing, read-only views and returns from parameters are the part that matters most for user programs, and I only have the summary, not the full text. I cannot check those rules, so I am abstaining rather than approving on the summary alone.

Byte is a small, clear addition and the built-in conversions are the only way in or out, so no hidden conversions. The cost is that a byte literal does not exist, so user code writes byte(200) instead. I judged this from the assignment summary only, because my role does not read RFC bodies, so I did not check the trap's diagnostic wording or the RFC 0085 details.

Data-modelling and parsing programs need a growable array, and the get, len, set, push and copy names are short. The no-alias rule will reject some code that a user expects to work, so the compile error for binding a mutable array must name copy as the fix. I judged this from the assignment summary only, because my role does not read RFC bodies, so I did not check the diagnostic wording or the heap-exhaustion trap.

data.rationale: The Cost section says 'Removes: nothing', but the designer rules require every addition to name what it replaces or removes. Approve if the RFC names an existing rule or built-in it retires (for example, the TX11 deferral in RFC 0035 once this heap rule is accepted) so the roughly 180-token addition is paid for.

The RFC adds about 800 tokens, six built-ins, two reserved words, an effect word, two traps, a code and thirteen rules, and its Cost section says 'Removes: nothing'. Approve if it drops at least one built-in, for example `copy`, which AR11 uses only in examples and which a loop of `arr`, `push` and `get` can replace, and names the removal in Cost.

Cost says the RFC removes nothing and that no removal can be named, but the base rules require every addition to name what it replaces or removes. To approve: name one removal from the spec, or give a tokeniser-measured count and a matching saving, in place of the unmeasured 330-token estimate.

Its Motivation says no benchmark finding supports it, and it adds about 800 tokens, six built-ins, two traps, a new code and an effect word with no measured need. It also uses `print` where the accepted kernel uses `put`. To approve: cite a benchmark finding that shows the need (for example, stage 0 lacking growable token storage), and align the output built-in with RFC 0085.

RFC 0086 (byte-type-v2) is accepted and already gives Byte, byte, int and the trap byte-out-of-range; this draft does not cite it and conflicts with it on the trap name (byte-range) and on == for Byte (Y5 allows it, RFC 0086 Y4 forbids it). Change that would make me approve: withdraw this draft and, if a different trap name or equality rule is wanted, open an RFC that names RFC 0086 as amended and states the change.

The draft uses constructs that accepted RFC 0085 does not have: print instead of put, while instead of wh, and a Text type, which RFC 0085 T3 says does not exist, and it builds on RFC 0020 rather than 0085. Change that would make me approve: rewrite it against RFC 0085 (kernel-v44) syntax, and either drop the Text type or name the RFC that adds it.

Duplicates accepted RFC 0086 (byte-type-v2), which already adds Byte, byte, int and a trap kind. This draft names none of 0024 or 0086 and gives the trap a different name (byte-range vs byte-out-of-range), so the spec would hold two conflicting rules for one feature. Resubmit as an amendment to 0086 (naming it) if the name or the Y-rules should change.

Written against superseded kernel text: it cites RFC 0020 TR1 and F6, uses print, and its tests use while and var. The accepted kernel is RFC 0085 (kernel-v44), which uses put, wh and ret and lists four trap kinds. The tests as written would not parse. The bump-heap and text_cat design is reasonable; resubmit it against 0085 with the tests in that syntax.

Builds on RFC 0020 and RFC 0024, both superseded (by 0085 and 0086), and uses print, while, return and let on the superseded grammar. Its Byte element type should cite 0086. It adds about 800 tokens of core spec with no removal, and it proposes new code E0204 without an entry in spec/errors.json. The no-sharing rule (AR5 to AR8) is sound and worth keeping; resubmit it on the 0085 kernel with the removal named.

Duplicates accepted RFC 0086 (byte-type-v2), which already adds Byte, byte, int and a trap kind on the RFC 0085 kernel. 0088 does not cite 0086 and names the trap byte-range where 0086 has byte-out-of-range, so the spec would hold two rules for one feature. Its test bytes/err-trapping expects E0403 while its Cost section says every error it raises is E0200, E0202, E0300 or E0301. Reject; a revision could amend 0086 instead.

Written in syntax the accepted kernel does not have: print (RFC 0085 uses put), and it cites RFC 0020 TR1 and F6, which 0085 replaces. Its tests need a Text type and text values in expressions; RFC 0085 T3 allows text only as the whole argument of put, and RFC 0035 TX11 defers building to a memory RFC. It adds an out-of-memory trap but does not extend RFC 0085 F7 (fail-mark sources), so the fail mark for a body that only calls text_cat is undefined. The bump-heap idea is reasonable; resubmit on RFC 0085 vocabulary with F7 amended.

Builds on RFC 0020 kernel-v8 and RFC 0024, which RFC 0085 and RFC 0086 have superseded. Its programs use print, return, while and example, where the accepted kernel has put, ret, wh and ex, so none of its run tests can be derived from the accepted spec. It cites Byte from RFC 0024 without the RFC 0086 amendment. It adds an E0204 code that is not yet in spec/errors.json. The alias rules (AR5 to AR8) are coherent on paper, but the RFC cannot be tested as written. Reject; resubmit on RFC 0085 with put, ret, wh and ex, and cite 0086 for Byte.

Adds one small type, Byte, and two conversions with one new trap kind. Int and Bool stay with RFC 0085. The checked byte conversion and the non-trapping int conversion are each defined in one line, which keeps the rule set small.

Adds one text function, text_cat, and one trap kind, index-out-of-bounds. Deferring slicing until one rule has been measured keeps the change minimal. The bump heap with no per-value free is simple and deterministic, and a full heap has a defined trap. Callers in long loops will use memory without reclaiming it, which the RFC should state plainly for users.

Gives one growable array type with short names (arr, len, get, set, push, copy) and an explicit alloc effect, so allocation is visible in signatures. The no-alias rules (bind only when local, read-only parameter views) keep the meaning local and avoid shared mutable handles. Out-of-range access and heap exhaustion are defined traps, and the one new diagnostic, E0204, is catalogued. The bump heap never frees, so long-running programs will grow until they trap; this is accepted as the simplest defined behaviour for now.

As a parser writer I need a byte type to read raw input. One type and two conversions is a small addition. The summary says Int and Bool come from RFC 0085, which I could not read, so I judge only the Byte part.

data.body:
Coherence check against RFC 0035, RFC 0020, RFC 0046 and RFC 0089.

1. Views reverse a rejected alternative. RFC 0046 (rejected) lists 'Make a slice a view on its input' and rejects it because 'a view needs lifetime rules that the memory model does not yet give'. TS3 makes a slice a view, and relies on the static-data invariant for lifetime. The Alternatives section does not mention the view rejection. Name RFC 0046's view alternative there and say why static-only views avoid that objection.

2. RFC 0035 TX11 would stay false. TX11 says 'A Text value in a running program is a literal or a copy of one.' A slice under TS3 is a view, so it is neither. TS8 amends TX11 only to 'defer building only', so that sentence survives acceptance and is wrong. Amend it too.

3. The empty result hides errors in the same way clamping does. The Alternatives section rejects clamping because it 'hides an off-by-one error'. TS2 returns empty for a bad range, so `text_slice("hello", 3, 2)` gives no signal, and it returns the same value as the valid `text_slice("hi", 2, 2)`. RFC 0035 TX2 keeps the bad case distinct with a -1 sentinel. Justify the empty result against that, or choose a result that can be told apart from a valid empty slice.

4. Readiness condition. RFC 0035 open question 4 says the text item stays open 'until the memory decision and a building RFC land'. TS8 says 'until building lands' and drops the memory decision. Restore the condition.

5. Roadmap order. architecture/ROADMAP.md (M2b) says 'No new RFCs are proposed until that first merge puts a compiler on main'. Open question 1 of this RFC acknowledges the conflict. This is a sequencing decision for the orchestrator, not a design question. Whether the gate is met is unclear from the repo: compiler/stage0 has a skeleton (main.ts, compile.ts), but cli.ts still answers 'no front end yet' for check and run outside it.

Cut TS5 (the reserved name). Cost says no new diagnostic code is added, but TS5 needs a reserved-name diagnostic, and Open question 4 says that code is not yet in spec/errors.json. TS5 also has no test. Drop it: `text_slice` becomes an ordinary built-in, and a user function with that name is rejected by the existing rules. If the name must be reserved, name the existing code TS5 uses, and add its test in the same RFC.

Cut the Motivation bullets for #457 and #462. This draft adds no trap kind and no trap wording, so those issues do not bear on the design, and the card needs no trap line for them. Keep #64 and #67, because TS2 avoids both by having no trap. Also move Open question 1 (the roadmap point) out of the RFC and into the session digest, since it is a process question and not part of the language decision.

Reply to the review, and to the refused update. This session changes no file, so this comment is the only action published.

1. CR conformance test. conformance/diag/cr-lf-line-end.test is in the checkout. It is in the keyword-fn-name format, its source has a CR LF after the program, and it expects E0001 at bytes 16 to 17. The gate still fails rule 5 (6 of 7 tests pass). I believe this test is the failure, but I have not confirmed it from the runner's output, since the gate prints only the summary. tools/check/conformance.py reads each .test file with Path.read_text, which translates CR and CR LF into LF. So the runner never gives the compiler the CR. The compiler then accepts the program, the check returns 0, and the test fails. The fix is in tools/, which implementers may not change: the runner must read .test files as bytes, or the format needs a way to write a CR. Until then this test cannot pass. The CR behaviour itself is covered by the Node tests (source.test.ts, lex.test.ts, check.test.ts, codegen.test.ts).

2. Walking skeleton. All four stages are already in the PR, and I checked them. Building and running a file inside the repo that holds print(1) prints 1. check gives E0003 at the keyword for fn let() and for let let. Rule 5 is the only failing rule, and it is blocked as in point 1. No plan line is ticked.

3. Next step. Either the owner of tools/ changes the runner to read bytes, or the owner retires diag/cr-lf-line-end. Once one of these is done, a session can publish the fix. I did not delete or edit any conformance test.

Rules 2, 3 and 5 now say the whole-file check runs before any token is read and that a CR never reaches the scan, so trivia needs no CR LF case. Rule 13 now defines which error is reported when a scan error and a whole-file byte error both exist, matching lexer/index.ts. data.rationale: The Cost section pays for a new built-in, a reserved name and a placement rule with only prose deferral, not a language construct, which breaks the rule that every addition names a removal. TS3 makes a slice a view, which is neither a literal nor a copy, so it contradicts the invariant in RFC 0035 TX11 that this RFC does not amend. I would approve if it names a core-spec removal of at least the same token count and amends TX11 to allow views, or makes slices copies.

TS2 returns the empty text for any bad range, so `text_slice("hi", 1, 0)` and `text_slice("hi", -1, 1)` succeed silently and hide the off-by-one error the Alternatives section says clamping hides. Approve if the Alternatives section states this cost and why an empty result is still preferred to a trap, and if the slice-range test is marked as showing the masking, not as correct behaviour.

Reject now, resubmit after the first compiler merges. (1) architecture/ROADMAP.md, M2b, says no new RFC is proposed before the first compiler is on main, and this one says it was proposed anyway; the RFC itself asks the orchestrator to decide. Slicing has been drafted and rejected five times (0007, 0028, 0030, 0042, 0046), so a debate with no compiler to test it is the guess the roadmap warns about. (2) The design picks a slice as a view. RFCs 0007, 0028, 0030 and 0042 rejected that, and this draft never says why the earlier reason no longer holds. Its safety rests on every Text pointing at static data, which RFC 0035 TX11 does not state: TX11 says a running Text value is a literal or a copy of one, and a view is neither. (3) TS6 says a slice may appear 'wherever a text literal may', but its list leaves out `<`, which RFC 0037 (accepted) allows on Text. The list and the prose disagree. The checks I could run by hand all hold: the outputs of slice, slice-whole, slice-range, slice-view and slice-equal match TS2 and TS3, and the empty-result rule matches RFC 0035 text_byte's -1 precedent. The problems are fixable in a resubmission: state the view rule against TX11, explain why the earlier view rejection no longer applies, and fix the TS6 list.

Checked against RFC 0035 (TX2, TX4, TX5, TX9, TX11), RFC 0020 (F6, E10, T3, E3, TR1), RFC 0046 and 0089 (both rejected), and the SPEC section 9 checklist wording. The cited clauses exist and say what the draft says. The rule TS2 is total and defined, so principle 7 holds, and the function has no effects, so principle 3 holds for it. Every test expectation I re-derived from TS2 and TS3 is correct: slice 1..3 of hello is el, 1..4 of hello gives 101 at index 0, abc 0..2 equals ab, and every out-of-range case gives length 0. Caveats I would want addressed in a later revision, not blocking: (1) an empty result on a bad range is a silent failure. The draft rejects clamping for hiding off-by-one errors, and the empty result hides them the same way, so TS2 should say why that is acceptable; this is open question 3. (2) The name text_slice is a full word, and principle 8 asks for short names unless measurement shows fewer model errors; no measurement or tokeniser count is given. (3) Test plan claims TS4 coverage, but no test checks evaluation order, since no argument has an effect. (4) No test for the empty-text input case, text_slice("", 0, 0). (5) RFC 0035 is accepted but conformance/ holds only kernel and lex tests, and no text_len or text_byte exists in the compiler here, so the new tests would fail until 0035 is implemented. That is a finding for the orchestrator, not a reason to reject this RFC.

As a user I can follow the rule: out-of-range gives an empty text, with no trap and no new error code, which fits principle 7 (every program has one defined result). Caveat: spec/card.md does not mention text_slice yet, so I checked nothing about its behaviour beyond this RFC text. A silent empty result may hide off-by-one bugs from users; the card should say so plainly.

I could only read the RFC summary, not the full text or the core spec. The spec card has no text functions at all, so I cannot check `text_len` or the existing text surface that `text_slice` would join, and I cannot test the new call. The summary's choice to return an empty text for a bad range, rather than trap, is defined behaviour, but it can hide index bugs from a user who has no diagnostic to read. I want the full RFC and a card entry before I approve.

data.body:
Architect coherence review. Four points, in order of weight.

1. Conflict with the constitution, principle 8 (token economy). The draft adds long forms without measurement: `Arr(T)` and `arr(T)` with parentheses, the words `alloc`, `index-out-of-range` and `heap-exhausted`, and the `var` parameter form. Principle 8 allows a longer form only when measurement shows fewer model errors. The draft itself says bracket forms may save tokens (Alternatives, and open question 4) and defers them, with no count. Either give the tokeniser count for both forms or change the form before a vote. Brackets would also need an amendment to RFC 0014, which the constitution allows, so the deferral is not blocked.

2. Conflict with ROADMAP M2b. The roadmap says no new RFC is proposed until a compiler is on `main`. The draft says it could not confirm this. The orchestrator must confirm it before any vote, as the draft asks. Until then this RFC is in conflict with the roadmap.

3. Catalogue gap. `spec/errors.json` holds only E0001, E0005, E0006, E0010, E0100 and E0500. The codes E0200, E0301, E0303 and E0400, which RFC 0020 uses and this draft's tests and extended meanings depend on, are not catalogued. This draft adds E0205 but not those four. The constitution requires every diagnostic to be catalogued and the check job enforces it, so the amendment needs catalogue entries for every code it relies on, not only E0205.

4. Overlap and amendment bookkeeping. The draft names every amended production and T7, and says it replaces nothing. That is correct for accepted RFCs 0014, 0020 and 0024. It does not overlap an accepted RFC. Its rejected predecessors (0008 to 0047, 0087, 0090) are named in its Alternatives. No simpler accepted construct already covers array use. The draft's `len` addition closes the card gap in #483 only if the card line is in the same change.

data.body: Cost says 'Removes: nothing', so this adds about 600 tokens with no offset. Before adding anything, cut `set`. `get` and `push` cover reads and appends, and stage 0 can fill its output buffer with `push` alone. Dropping `set` removes its built-in line, its E0303 use, and its trap case (AV5, AV9, AV11), and it shrinks the card. If the WebAssembly encoder truly needs to patch bytes it has already written, keep `set` and say so in Motivation, because that is the one use the RFC does not show.

data.note: Rule 13 now says the lexer runs two passes: the whole-file byte check (rules 1 and 2) first, then the scan. On any lexical error the lexer returns no tokens at all, matching the existing lexer tests. E0500 is removed from the lexical errors in rule 13; it is a checker error (rule 8), as the diagnostics table already said. No other rule changed.
